issues.title: DeepSeek search backend works end to end but has no parser test, unlike every other API backend

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: web-search
labels.description: Web search tool, search backends, result parsing, and browser/fetch search UX

labels.name: tools
labels.description: Tool execution, tool schemas, tool UX, and built-in tool behavior

labels.name: v0.10.2
labels.description: Targeting v0.10.2

issues.body:
## Summary

The DeepSeek Search backend shipped in `85688ac230` (an ancestor of the 0.10.2
candidate `cc4b96dc`). It **works**: verified against the live API and through
Codewhale's own `Web` tool. The gap is regression cover — `parse_deepseek_results`
has no test, while every other API-backed backend has one.

## What was verified (2026-10-21)

Contract checked against <https://api-docs.deepseek.com/guides/search>:

| Piece | Location | State |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Provider variant | `config/search.rs:68` | serde `deepseek`, aliases `deep-seek`, `deepseek-search` |
| Endpoint | `tools/web_search.rs:45` | `https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search` — matches docs |
| Request | `tools/web_search.rs:1204` | `{query: first 128 chars, count: clamp(1,50)}` — matches docs (query 1–128, count 1–50) |
| Response parser | `tools/web_search.rs:3143` | `results[].title`, `url`, `snippet` else `summary`, `date` |
| Key resolution | `tools/web_search.rs:1868` | `[search] api_key`, then `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` |
| Preflight | `tools/web_search.rs:1923` | fails closed with a named remedy |

Live API call — `POST /v1/tools/search`, `{"query":"…","count":3}`:

```
HTTP=200  time=0.66s
results: 3
item keys: ['title','site_name','site_icon','authority','rerank_score',
            'date','url','summary','snippet','content']
```

Through our own tool — `codewhale exec` on `deepseek-flash` with
`[search] provider = "deepseek"`:

```
"source":"deepseek"  "count":5  "message":"Found 5 result(s)"
results[0]: crates.io: Rust Package Registry / https://crates.io/crates/codewhale/0.9.1
receipt: backend=deepseek, latency_ms=575, cache_hit=false
capabilities: max_results=supported, recency=unsupported, domains=unsupported,
              locale=unsupported, published_date=unknown
```

The capability receipt is honest about what the backend does not do.

## The gap

```
parse_bocha_results_reads_*                                  (2 tests)
parse_serply_results_reads_link_and_description_and_skips_malformed_rows
parse_tavily_results …
parse_baidu_results / metaso / searxng / sofya / volcengine
```

`parse_deepseek_results` has **none**. The parser is the piece most likely to
break silently: if DeepSeek renamed `summary` or a row arrived without `url`,
`filter_map` would drop it and the tool would report **zero results** rather
than an error. The live call above proves today's shape, not tomorrow's.

Suggested cases, mirroring the serply test:

- reads `title` + `url` + `snippet`, and falls back to `summary` when `snippet`
  is empty;
- skips rows missing `title` or `url` instead of emitting blanks;
- honours `max_results` and numbers ranks from 1;
- an empty/missing `results` array is an empty vec, not a panic.

## Also fixed alongside

`config.example.toml` never listed the backend — the provider list, the
description block, the "needs an api_key" sentence and the `api_key` comment all
stopped at `serply`, so a user reading the example could not discover it.
`docs/CONFIGURATION.md` did have it. Fixed on `main` as `7719b717d2`.

## Not proven

macOS CLI only; no Windows/Linux, no desktop/web surface, and no hosted CI
(final release step).

issues.title: Runtime split RS-14: move the strongly connected runtime core into codewhale-runtime (one rename-only change)

labels.name: agent-ready
labels.description: Self-contained for a fresh-clone cloud agent; implement in a tested PR with no live credentials

labels.name: cleanup
labels.description: Code cleanup, refactor, or maintenance work

labels.name: tui
labels.description: Terminal UI behavior, rendering, or interaction

issues.body:
Part of the runtime/TUI crate split. Read first: `docs/design/TUI_DECONSTRUCTION.md` — in particular the "runtime split sequence" and "Where this sequence departs" sections. This is the keystone change the rest of the series exists to enable: the runtime half of `crates/tui` is **one strongly connected component** (verified with `scripts/split/module_graph.py` on 2026-10-09: 82 modules, ~792,000 LOC, SCC confirmed over production edges alone), and a crate cannot hold half a cycle. So it moves in one rename-only change, after every upward reference is gone.

**Do not start until the ratchet is zero.** Run `python3 scripts/split/module_graph.py --check`; all categories — `prod`, `test`, `late`, `uilib`, `doc` — must be 0 after RS-8..RS-13. A partial move does not compile; there is no halfway state.

## Goal

Move the runtime closure out of `crates/tui/src/` into `crates/runtime/src/` (`codewhale-runtime`) in one `git mv`-dominated change, with the TUI keeping resolvable `crate::<module>` paths through its single alias block (`crates/tui/src/lib.rs:143-152`).

## Plan

1. Regenerate the authoritative member list: `python3 scripts/split/module_graph.py --report` and take `closure`, minus modules already resident in `crates/runtime`. As of 2026-10-09 that is the 82-module list. At execution time the tool's output is the authority, not this issue.
2. Resolve the non-closure stragglers the ratchet names:
   - `exec_agent` — the only `late` entry is `crates/tui/src/core/engine/tests/test_cases_04.rs:1197` using `crate::exec_agent::ExecAgentEvents`; `exec_agent`'s production dependencies are all inside the closure, so include it in the moving batch.
   - `conformance` — `#[cfg(test)]`-gated, used by `crates/tui/src/extension_host/protocol/tests.rs:471`. Both must live in the same crate's test build; the batch moves both.
   - `computer_meter` — deliberately held back from RS-10 because it is `pub mod`. See the public-surface step below.
3. Land any still-needed private-visibility or rustdoc edits in place first (a reviewable prep change), so the move itself is rename-only.
4. Move the batch with `scripts/split/move-modules.py <modules…>` (it `git mv`s, rewrites `mod` lines, extends the alias block, sweeps path strings across the repo). Then run `scripts/split/widen.py` until the compiler's privacy errors are resolved — it widens only the definitions the compiler names, and flags security-relevant widening for human review.
5. **Public surface.** `codewhale-tui` is published to crates.io (see #6910 for the tarball-cap context). Inventory its public items before moving any: today's `pub mod` list is `agent_roster`, `cloud_dispatch`, `computer_meter`, `config_keys`, `delivery_files`, `dispatch_runner`, `reasoning_preference`, `repl`, `rlm`, `route_preferences`, plus crate-root `pub` fns. For each, either keep it in the TUI or keep the published path resolving via a compat re-export that names the external contract (the repo rule allows this only for genuine external contracts; label it). Get a maintainer decision before breaking the published API in a patch cycle.
6. Ratchet: after the move, `scripts/split/module_graph.py --check` must still pass; run `--update` — the baseline goes to zero. Keep the gate in CI: a zero baseline is the standing guard that the runtime crate never grows a new upward reference.
7. **Do not delete the alias in this change.** Follow-on, separate PR: rewrite `crate::<module>` paths in `crates/tui/src` to `codewhale_runtime::<module>` and remove the alias block, then delete the shim. The doc specifies exactly this order so in-flight branches can rebase across the move.

## Done when

- [ ] The closure modules live under `crates/runtime/src/`; `crates/tui/src` keeps only UI code (`tui/`, `commands/`, `remote_control`, `context_report`, `composer_*`, `lib.rs`, `main.rs`) plus the moved batch's alias names
- [ ] The change is rename-dominated: `git diff --stat -M` shows renames, not rewrites. Contents are unchanged except mod lines, the alias block, visibility widening, and swept path strings
- [ ] Model-facing contracts are preserved: prompt/cache-prefix semantics, tool names and order, serialized records, public commands
- [ ] The headless runtime and its tests build with **no transitive dependency on `codewhale-tui`, ratatui, or crossterm**
- [ ] Ratchet `--check` passes with a zeroed baseline committed
- [ ] Warmed edit/build/test cycles are measured before and after for a provider edit, a tool edit, a renderer edit, and a locale edit, with compiler/profile/features/cache state recorded (template: `docs/BUILD_PERFORMANCE.md`)

## Verification

```sh
scripts/dev-cargo.sh check --workspace --all-targets --locked
scripts/dev-test.sh runtime
scripts/dev-test.sh tui
scripts/dev-test.sh cli
cargo build --release -p codewhale-cli -p codewhale-tui
python3 scripts/split/module_graph.py --check
git diff --stat -M
```

Also run the behavioural set the plan names at the affected boundaries: mock-provider parent and child turns, tool approval and denial, streaming, cancel/steer, explicit goals, pause/resume, reconnect, restart recovery, terminal fan-in. Local tests, full gates, hosted CI, installed artifacts, and PTY behaviour are separate evidence — report them separately. Quote the real `test result: N passed; M failed` lines and the ratchet `PASS` line.

## Out of scope

- Any behaviour change; any file's contents rewritten beyond the mechanical edits above
- Deleting the path alias (separate follow-up PR)
- Peeling sub-crates out of `codewhale-runtime` (models, tools, mcp, hooks, config) — post-move internal work with its own plan; do not start it here
- New tests or new code comments (repo rule)

## Coordination

This change touches nearly every file in two crates. Before starting, confirm no other writer holds the shared checkout for the affected paths (`AGENTS.md`, "Working rules"), and land it as one PR.

---

**Series:** RS-8 #6935 · RS-9 #6936 · RS-10 #6937 · RS-11 #6938 · RS-12 #6939 · RS-13 #6940 · RS-14 #6941 (keystone; blocked by the rest). Umbrella: #5316.

issues.body:
Part of the runtime/TUI crate split. Read first: `docs/design/TUI_DECONSTRUCTION.md` and the mover `scripts/split/move-modules.py` (it `git mv`s a top-level module, edits the `mod` lines, adds the name to the TUI's single path-alias block in `crates/tui/src/lib.rs:143-152`, and sweeps stale path strings). A lowercase reading of this task is "move small files"; the point is that these are **runtime-side subsystems with already-clean boundaries** — process supervision, shell dispatch, credentials exchange, runtime policy/logging, feature registry — that belong in the headless crate and will grow there.

Run slices one at a time — do not stack two `RS-n` slices in one working tree.

## Goal

Move ten modules from `crates/tui/src/` into `crates/runtime/src/`. Each one has **zero upward references** today (verified by `scripts/split/module_graph.py --report`), so no ratchet entry changes; their only dependencies are modules already resident in `crates/runtime` (or each other):

- `child_env` (1,423 lines) — no deps
- `logging` (134) — no deps
- `external_credentials` (938) — no deps
- `dsh_credentials` (148) — depends on `external_credentials` (moves in this batch)
- `shell_dispatcher` (994) — depends on `host_terminal` (already in runtime)
- `runtime_policy` (167) — no deps
- `process_tree` (935) — no deps
- `features` (375) — no deps
- `runtime_log` (588) — no deps
- `working_set` (2,505) — depends on `workspace_discovery` (already in runtime)

## Plan

1. Dry-run first: `python3 scripts/split/move-modules.py --dry-run child_env logging external_credentials dsh_credentials shell_dispatcher runtime_policy process_tree features runtime_log working_set` — read the printed path sweep. `--dry-run` writes nothing.
2. Run it for real, one module list in one change.
3. `crates/tui/tests/feature_registry.rs:10` carries `#[path = "../src/features.rs"] mod features;`. Update the include to the new location (`../../runtime/src/features.rs`) or switch the test to the runtime export if `features` is made `pub` there. Keep `cargo test -p codewhale-tui --test feature_registry` green — it is the `docs/features.toml` drift guard and must keep failing on flag drift.
4. `grep -rn 'crates/tui/src/\(child_env\|logging\|external_credentials\|dsh_credentials\|shell_dispatcher\|runtime_policy\|process_tree\|features\|runtime_log\|working_set\)' --include='*.rs'` must be empty (the sweep leaves CHANGELOG history alone; that is intended).
5. `python3 scripts/split/module_graph.py --check` — totals must be unchanged (these modules never counted). If a count moved, a real reference appeared; fix it, do not raise the baseline.
6. `scripts/split/widen.py` only if the compiler reports privacy errors from the move.

## Done when

- [ ] The ten modules live under `crates/runtime/src/` with `pub mod` lines in `crates/runtime/src/lib.rs`; the TUI's `mod` lines are gone and the alias block names all ten
- [ ] `crates/tui/src` no longer contains these files; no stale path strings outside CHANGELOG
- [ ] `cargo check` for both crates is clean and `feature_registry` passes
- [ ] Ratchet `--check` passes with **no** baseline edit

## Verification

```sh
scripts/dev-cargo.sh check -p codewhale-runtime --all-targets --locked
scripts/dev-cargo.sh check -p codewhale-tui --all-targets --locked
scripts/dev-test.sh runtime
scripts/dev-test.sh tui features
cargo test -p codewhale-tui --test feature_registry --locked
python3 scripts/split/module_graph.py --check
```

Quote the real `test result: N passed; M failed` lines and the ratchet `PASS` line in the PR.

## Out of scope

- `conformance` — it is `#[cfg(test)]`-gated and its user (`extension_host/protocol/tests.rs:471`) is also in the runtime closure; a cross-crate `cfg(test)` module is invisible to the other crate's test build, so it moves together with its user in RS-14
- `test_support` — carries `#[cfg(test)]` and UI fixtures; that split is RS-11
- `computer_meter` — it is `pub mod` today, i.e. a published-surface decision; handle it in RS-14's public-surface inventory
- Behaviour changes anywhere; new re-exports; new tests or comments (repo rule)

The installed Engine can retain a dead local owner publication and refuse the next native-app startup, leaving the app offline until an operator repairs task-owned metadata. issues.body:
## Background

Codewhale's agent memory is currently a hardwired, single-implementation native feature with no pluggable third-party backend entry:

- The `MemoryBackend` enum has only `Native` / `Off` variants (`crates/tui/src/config.rs:1985`) — no `Custom`/`External`/`MCP`.
- `NativeMemoryStore` (`crates/tui/src/native_memory.rs:51`) is a concrete struct (Markdown source + SQLite FTS5 index) with no trait, so a third party cannot supply their own store.
- The plugin activation capability list `PluginActivationCapability` (`crates/tui/src/plugins/activation.rs:26`) has no `Memory` category, so a plugin cannot declare "I provide a memory backend".
- `docs/MEMORY.md` states that native is the only memory system, the planned Moraine MCP backend was removed, and `backend` accepts only `native` / `off`.

Today a third-party memory system can only be side-mounted through the generic MCP channel (most external memory systems expose an MCP server). It can be wired in, but it is not a first-class backend recognized by `[memory]` — `# quick-add`, the `remember` tool, and the `/memory` command all remain pinned to native.

## Goal

Upgrade memory from "single, hardwired implementation" to a **generic, pluggable, optional** seam:

- Keep native as the default, zero-dependency local backend.
- Define a stable backend seam that **any** third-party memory system can implement — not one tailored to a particular vendor.
- Make `[memory] backend` a first-class config choice, with the existing `remember` / recall / `/memory` lifecycle routing to whichever backend is selected; a backend only implements "store" and "retrieve".
- Ship causal-memory and mem0 as the **first two reference implementations** to prove the seam is generic across very different backend shapes — not as the endpoint of the work.

## The seam is open to any memory system

The abstraction is deliberately transport- and vendor-agnostic, so the following (and others) can all be implemented behind the same interface:

- **causal-memory** — causal/decision memory (local, MCP stdio/HTTP).
- **mem0** — fact/preference recall (remote service, API/SDK + MCP).
- **Zep, Letta (MemGPT), LangMem, MemOS, Mem0** — any agent-memory platform exposing a service API or MCP.
- A custom in-house store — implement the trait directly.

The only requirement is that a backend can answer "store an entry" and "retrieve relevant entries for a query".

## Reference implementation #1 (focus): causal-memory (developed in-house)

causal-memory is our open-source agent memory system (Rust, Apache-2.0, `JingxuanC/causal-memory`). Its core differentiator is a **causal core + inhibition modeling**: facts, temporal state, and `decision → outcome` causal edges live on a single SQLite store, driven by a hippocampus-style engine (typed spreading activation with excitatory *and* inhibitory edges, Hebbian co-occurrence reinforcement, Q-value dynamics, immutable SWR consolidation). Agents recall not only *what* happened and *when* it was true, but *why* it worked and *what would happen if* they acted differently.

Why it is the first backend we build:

1. **Causal information is the most fragile type under text compaction.** The causal table lives outside the agent's context window, so compaction cannot touch it — in a real-LLM compaction benchmark causal-memory retains 100% causal-table recall while mem0 drops to 45%. This directly patches the "re-hits the same bug the same wrong way" hole after long-session compaction.
2. **Clearly ahead of mem0 on causal capabilities** (CausalEval): C7 belief update 100% vs 80%, C2 intervention prediction 75% vs 40%, C4 inhibition distinction 80% vs 50%.
3. **Integration surface is ready**: 14 MCP tools (stdio + HTTP transports), a Python `Memory` facade, and an existing DSH plugin shape — wiring into Codewhale's MCP/plugin channel is nearly zero new code.
4. The honest caveat: pure fact recall (LoCoMo 79.1% vs mem0 91.6%) is not its strong suit — that is exactly mem0's strength. The two are complementary, which is why a generic seam beats "pick one".

## Reference implementation #2: mem0

mem0 is the fact-recall specialist (LoCoMo 91.6%) and is chosen as the second reference implementation precisely because its shape is the opposite of causal-memory's: a **remote hosted service** with an API/SDK, rather than a local store. If the seam can absorb both, it is general enough for the rest of the ecosystem.

## Plan (phased)

- **Phase 0 — baseline (already landed)**: native as the only backend, `[memory]` opt-in, `#` quick-add, `remember`/recall tools. Landed in v0.9.x.
- **Phase 1 — define the generic backend seam (core change)**: introduce a `MemoryBackend` trait with a minimal, transport-agnostic method set (`store` / `search` / `prompt_block`, plus a health/`status` probe); add an `External`/`Custom` variant to the `MemoryBackend` enum; make `[memory] backend` resolve a backend by **kind + connection parameters** (process/stdio command, HTTP service URL, or MCP server name) rather than hardcoding vendor names. Native becomes a default impl of the trait; `Off` stays as-is. Add a `Memory` capability to `PluginActivationCapability` so a backend can ship as a plugin bundle.
- **Phase 2 — two reference implementations to prove genericity**: land **causal-memory** first (MCP stdio + HTTP), then **mem0** (remote API/SDK). Success criterion: the trait needed no vendor-specific escape hatches to absorb two very different backend shapes.
- **Phase 3 — bring-your-own-backend**: document the driver/adaptor contract so any third party (Zep, Letta, LangMem, a custom store, …) can add a backend — ideally as an external plugin bundle, without a core change.
- **Phase 4 — wrap-up**: update `docs/MEMORY.md`, `config.example.toml`, and the `[memory]` config contract; add backend selection + fallback (degrade to off or native when a backend is unavailable); document the KV-cache effect (the boundary of memory injected into the system-prompt prefix is unchanged).

## Integration surface

- **Reuse the existing MCP/plugin channel**: causal-memory is already an MCP server and can land first as a plugin bundle (`McpStdio`/`McpRemote`) as the Phase 2 bootstrap — no need to wait for the trait abstraction before trying it out. Any MCP-speaking memory system gets the same path for free.
- **Add a native trait backend**: make `[memory] backend = "causal-memory"` (or any registered backend) a first-class config option, with the `remember` tool, `/memory` command, and `#` quick-add all routing to the selected backend.
- **Open the plugin capability**: a `Memory` activation capability lets a third party ship a backend as a reviewed plugin, exactly like they ship skills, MCP servers, or hooks today.

## References

- Current memory implementation: `crates/tui/src/native_memory.rs`, `crates/tui/src/config.rs` (`MemoryBackend` / `MemoryConfig`)
- Memory docs: `docs/MEMORY.md`
- Plugin activation capabilities: `crates/tui/src/plugins/activation.rs`
- causal-memory: https://github.com/JingxuanC/causal-memory (README includes the CausalEval / compaction-survival benchmarks)
- Original memory EPIC: #489

prs.title: fix(shell): preserve Python stdio env defaults
prs.body:
## Summary
Preserve constructor environment defaults when shell execution overlays an empty or unrelated hook/task map. The overlay is unconditional on ordinary shell execution, including when no hook/task variables are supplied. Previously `with_env` replaced the entire map, dropping Windows `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`; Python emitted locale-encoded bytes while PowerShell decoded UTF-8, corrupting Python Chinese output even when PowerShell Chinese remained correct.

Merge overlays and replace existing Windows keys case-insensitively. Explicit overrides and child-environment sanitization remain effective. Python file/default-text encoding is unchanged. Extend the existing builder test for empty/unrelated overlays, explicit overrides, and Windows key casing.

## Verification
- `cargo test -p codewhale-tui --lib --locked sandbox::tests -- --test-threads=1`: **23 passed, 0 failed** on native Windows at `e59226e`. Cargo matches this filter as a substring: **17 `sandbox::tests::*` tests plus 6 `repl::sandbox::tests::*` tests**.
- Rust formatting and whitespace checks passed.
- The equivalent maintenance-fork fix additionally passed native foreground/background Python stdout/stderr regressions with system Python 3.14 and bundled Python 3.13.14; restoring the old environment builders made both tests fail with each interpreter. These are local author executions in the maintenance fork, not executions of those additional tests in this upstream PR.
- The Windows execution evidence above is local. Current upstream checks report DCO and gate success; this does not establish that a native Windows encoding lane ran. The maintenance fork's `pinvou3-clean` CI is Ubuntu-only and does not execute Windows-gated regressions. Any future upstream Windows CI execution should be assessed separately from this local evidence.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 was exercised; PowerShell 7, customer-machine replay, and an installer build were not run. Pre-existing direct `CommandSpec::program` consumers, including the hardened read-only Python lane and `codew sandbox run`, do not seed the shell-specific default and are outside this fix's claim.

This is an upstream contribution from the Pinvou maintenance fork, not a release. Maintenance implementation and additional regressions: https://github.com/Pinvou/CodeWhale/pull/115. Parent integration: https://github.com/Pinvou/pinvou-agent/pull/750.

No-Issue: Windows Python stdio defect reported through the downstream project; maintenance tracking is Pinvou/CodeWhale#115 and parent integration is Pinvou/pinvou-agent#750.

Paulo Aboim Pinto

prs.title: fix(tui): keep a to-do row's status word when its title is long
prs.body:
## What and why

The work surface gives a row's label the whole width and the detail only what is left, and drops the detail under four columns. A to-do whose title fills the strip loses its status word. With a three-step to-do list at 80×24, before:

```
 To-do · 1/3 · 2 left
 1 · ✓ Read the README to learn the layout                            completed
 2 · ▸ Search the workspace for every README and compare their install secti...
 3 · ○ Write up the differences                                         pending
```

After:

```
 To-do · 1/3 · 2 left
 1 · ✓ Read the README to learn the layout                            completed
 2 · ▸ Search the workspace for every README and compare their ...  in progress
 3 · ○ Write up the differences                                         pending
```

The step that lost its word is the in-progress one, the row most worth reading. `todo_rows_carry_their_status_words` already pins that the words are projected and painted; this keeps them painted when the title is long. Plan-step (to-do) rows, picked by the same `plan_step_row_ids` set the strip's filter uses, now reserve the detail's width, capped at half the row, before the title is truncated. A title that fits renders as before, and the hover still carries the full title.

Other rows keep giving the label the room. I tried the reservation on every row first, and at 60 columns the Context budget row cut its numbers (`6.5k of 128.0k · 5% · com...`) to show more of the `/context for the full source map` hint, so it stays on to-do rows only. The first version keyed on the `graph:` id prefix; on a side rail that also matched the operation and blocker nodes listed under the to-dos, so the second commit checks the plan-step ids instead and those rows keep the label-first layout. Background task rows (`status · id`) aren't changed either.

## Issue

No-Issue: a long to-do title drops its status word in the work surface; I searched and found no issue for it

## How I tested it

- Ran a debug build in a pseudo-terminal with an empty HOME against a local OpenAI-compatible mock that answers with `read`, `file_search` and a three-item `todo_write`, with this change and with a build from before it. The screens above are 80×24. At 60×16 the in-progress row goes from `Search the workspace for every README and compare...` to `Search the workspace for every READM...  in progress`; at 48×16 row 1 goes from `...` in place of its word to `completed`, and row 2 gains `in progress`. At 120×30, where the titles fit, the strip is unchanged.
- Walked the Cost, Git, Context and Files tabs at 80×24 and 60×16 with both builds: identical.
- With `work_surface_placement = "left"` and a 60-column rail, main drops `in progress` from the long row and this shows it; the `Read 1 files · Searched 1 patterns` row under the to-dos is unchanged. The strip rows are the same with and without the second commit. I couldn't get the mock to produce an operation or blocker node, so for those rows I'm relying on the id check: they take the same path as on main.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy -p codewhale-tui --all-targets --all-features` with CI's flags, and `cargo check -p codewhale-tui --all-targets`: clean. Clippy also on 1.99, plus `cargo +1.89.0 check -p codewhale-tui`.
- `cargo nextest run -p codewhale-tui --lib`: 15347 passed, none failed, including the work surface tests and the shared-body-vs-frozen-body comparison.

prs.title: fix(tui): keep nested list indentation in rendered markdown
prs.body:
## What and why

The transcript's markdown parser trims each line before it looks for a list marker and keeps only the marker and the text, so a nested list renders flat. A reply with

```
- Top level item
  - Second level, indented two spaces
    - Third level, indented four spaces, long enough to wrap at forty columns
- Another top level item

1. Step one
   - detail a under step one
   - detail b under step one
2. Step two
```

renders at 80×24, before:

```
▏ - Top level item
▏ - Second level, indented two spaces
▏ - Third level, indented four spaces, long enough to wrap at forty columns
▏ - Another top level item
▏
▏ 1. Step one
▏ - detail a under step one
▏ - detail b under step one
▏ 2. Step two
```

After:

```
▏ - Top level item
▏   - Second level, indented two spaces
▏     - Third level, indented four spaces, long enough to wrap at forty
▏       columns
▏ - Another top level item
▏
▏ 1. Step one
▏    - detail a under step one
▏    - detail b under step one
▏ 2. Step two
```

Before, the details under "1." read like siblings of the numbered steps. `ListItem` now records the source line's leading whitespace and the renderer paints it before the bullet, so wrapped rows still hang under the item's text. The indent is capped at half the width so a pathological line can't push the text out of the pane. Lists without leading whitespace render as before.

What it doesn't do: a list item's own continuation line in the source (`- item` then an indented line of prose) is still a paragraph and renders flush left, and a tab counts as one column. A top-level list the model indents by one to three spaces now shifts right by that much, since the renderer paints what was written.

## Issue

No-Issue: nested markdown lists render flat in the transcript; I searched and found no issue for it

## How I tested it

- Ran a debug build in a pseudo-terminal with an empty HOME against a local OpenAI-compatible mock that streams a canned reply, with this change and with a build from before it. The screens above are from the nested reply at 80×24; 40×12 shows the same indentation. A reply whose lists all start at column 0 (`-`, `*`, `1.` to `10.`, with wrapped items) renders the same list rows before and after at 80×24 and 40×12. In a longer reply, `   - nested bullet` under `2. Second item` now sits under "Second item", with its wrapped path row under it.
- Checked that nothing outside `crates/tui/src` matches on `ListItem`.
- `cargo fmt --all -- --check`, `cargo clippy -p codewhale-tui --all-targets --all-features` with CI's flags, and `cargo check -p codewhale-tui --all-targets`: clean. Clippy also on 1.99, plus `cargo +1.89.0 check -p codewhale-tui`.
- `cargo nextest run -p codewhale-tui --lib`: 15347 passed, none failed, including the markdown render tests and the incremental-vs-full reparse test, whose corpus has a nested list.

## Checklist

- [x] One focused change, on cc4b96dc0; it merges cleanly into current `main`
- [x] `cargo fmt --all` passes, and tests cover new or changed behavior
- [ ] If this adds or changes a user-facing feature, I updated its docs and its row in `docs/features.toml` (`cargo test -p codewhale-tui --test feature_registry` checks it) — n/a

prs.title: fix(tui): put the approval footer's separators between its hints
prs.body:
## What and why

The approval card's footer starts with a dangling dot and runs its last hint into the one before it. A `bash` approval at 100×30, before:

```
❯ [3 / d / n] Don't allow (Enter)
  [Esc] Stop this turn
    ·  Pg↑/↓ review  ·  ⌥V details  ·  Esc stop  s allow now, and always ask before this again
```

After:

```
❯ [3 / d / n] Don't allow (Enter)
  [Esc] Stop this turn
  Pg↑/↓ review  ·  ⌥V details  ·  Esc stop  ·  s allow now, and always ask before this again
```

`ApprovalControlsHint` still opens with the `  ·  ` that once joined it to the "Choose: ..." prose; the per-option key badges replaced that prose, and the footer now starts its own line. `ApprovalSaveAskRuleHint`, appended right after it, has only two spaces, so "Esc stop  s allow now" reads as one item. This moves the separator from the front of `ApprovalControlsHint` and `ApprovalControlsHintChild` to the front of `ApprovalSaveAskRuleHint`, in all 15 packs, so the line starts at the option rows' column. Nothing else in the strings changes. A child agent's card already joins its `g go to agent` hint with `  ·  ` in `child_footer_controls`.

What it doesn't do: when the footer wraps (80 columns and narrower), the second row still starts at column 0. That wrapping is in the vendored `DecisionBand`, which I left alone.

## Issue

No-Issue: the approval footer's separators are misplaced; I searched and found no issue for it

## How I tested it

- Ran a debug build in a pseudo-terminal with an empty HOME against a local OpenAI-compatible mock that asks to run a `bash` command, with this change and with a build from before it. The screens above are 100×30. At 80×24 and 60×20 the footer reads the same way before it wraps, and under `LC_ALL=zh_TW.UTF-8` it reads `Pg↑/↓ 回看  ·  ⌥V 詳情  ·  Esc 停止  ·  s 本次允許，以後每次先詢問`. issues.body:
## Summary

Since upgrading to 2026.9.6 (`eb377ac`) the `prepared-model-catalog.worker.js` thread grows by roughly 1 GiB every 5 minutes with no user action, reaches 8 to 13 GiB, and the gateway's memory-pressure reclamation then resets it to under 2 GiB. Each reclamation supersedes the prepared runtime publication, and every agent turn that is waiting on that publication at that moment fails with:

```
prepared model runtime publication was superseded for <home>/.openclaw/agents/main/agent
```

The cycle repeats about once an hour all day, so users on several sessions see the same failure at the same second across tabs. This never happened on the previous version with the same sessions and workload.

## Environment

- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (`eb377ac`), upgraded 2026-09-27 from the build installed 2026-09-15
- macOS 26.6.2 Apple Silicon (Mac Studio), Node v26.5.0, npm install, launchd with `--max-old-space-size=9216`
- 22 agents, 9 providers, 13 plugins allowed, 8 cron jobs
- Main runtime is `claude-cli` for Anthropic models; a Codex-backed agent also present
- Several large sessions (one at roughly 900K tokens of history)

## Evidence: catalog worker heap over one day (from `memory pressure` log lines, `workerHeaps`)

```
time   level     rss       prepared-model-catalog.worker.js heapUsed
00:00  critical  8.59 GiB  7.62 GiB
00:38  warning   11.7 GiB  11.11 GiB
01:08  warning   13.8 GiB  13.44 GiB
01:33  warning   4.56 GiB  2.42 GiB   <- reclaimed
02:14  critical  9.56 GiB  8.23 GiB
02:24  warning   4.64 GiB  1.85 GiB   <- reclaimed
03:09  critical  10.9 GiB  8.42 GiB
03:16  warning   4.59 GiB  1.74 GiB   <- reclaimed
... same sawtooth every 45 to 60 min through the day ...
10:38  warning   6.53 GiB  4.46 GiB
10:51  warning   4.70 GiB  2.60 GiB   <- reclaimed
11:01  warning   5.82 GiB  4.51 GiB
11:23  critical  8.81 GiB  7.29 GiB
```

Growth is steady at about 200 MiB per minute regardless of chat activity. The main-thread heap stays around 600 MiB the whole time; the growth is entirely inside the catalog worker. Only two `models.list` requests were made all day, so it is not client polling.

## Evidence: a reclamation kills a waiting run (2026-09-28)

```
11:01:56.587 memory pressure: level=warning reason=rss_threshold rss=5.82 GiB heap=565.9 MiB threshold=4.55 GiB workerCount=9
             workerHeaps=[{"script":"prepared-model-catalog.worker.js","heapUsed":4846979712,"heapTotal":4902010880}, ...]
11:03:23.281 {'reclamationKind': 'maintenance-plan', 'workerThreadId': 76, 'elapsedMs': 1436, 'outcome': 'resolved'}
11:03:26.030 message dispatch completed: channel=webchat sessionKey=agent:main:... source=replyResolver outcome=error duration=47453ms
             error="Error: prepared model runtime publication was superseded for <home>/.openclaw/agents/main/agent"
```

Note this one fired at `level=warning`, not `critical`, so the kill happens well below the critical line. Earlier in the day the same error landed at 02:17 and 09:20 during `level=critical` reclaims, each time hitting every session that had a message in preparation.

## What I ruled out

- Invalid `models.json` cost blocks triggering catalog reloads: fixed locally, errors continued.
- Heartbeat auth-cooldown writes to config: heartbeats disabled, errors continued.
- Skills workshop autonomous review jobs: set to propose, errors continued.
- Config hot-reload (#144291): no config edits around the 11:03 event.
- Raising `--max-old-space-size` to 20480 to move the critical line: the gateway crashed at startup; reverted.
- An external idle-only restart guard: the worker refills in 15 to 20 minutes, so it just restarts constantly. Removed as an approach.

## Expected

The prepared-model-catalog worker should not grow without bound, and reclaiming or rebuilding it should not abort turns that are waiting on the current publication (they should either wait for the next publication or be retried, as #144291 asks for the config-reload case).

## Related

- #157107 (closed): catalog worker rebuilding the plugin generation every 6 s on 2026.9.6. Possibly the same worker behaviour, but on this install the rebuild is silent and shows up only as heap growth.
- #158127: superseded publication on Codex turns after 2026.9.6.
- #144291: same error text on config hot-reload.

A full `openclaw diagnostics` export (8 files, 71 KiB) from 2026-09-28 is available on request.

issues.body:
### Bug type

Performance regression / slow startup

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

On this Windows host the Gateway's plugin-load phase (`plugins.runtime-post-bind`, 23 plugins) takes **59,959.9 ms**, and **57.4 s of that is three channel plugins alone**. The cost is **module compilation**, not plugin logic: a single heavy channel plugin's entry costs **5.0 s (weixin)** to **7.4–13.2 s (feishu)** to import in a cold Node process, while its third-party SDK is **264 ms at most**. Pre-warming only the `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` subpaths those plugins import drops the same import to **224–448 ms** (weixin: 5.0 s → 0.22 s, a 22x difference).

So the dominant startup cost is re-compiling a large shared `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` module graph, once per plugin instance, on the Gateway's single main thread. Related: #159499 (two sequential registry phases; this report isolates what one of them is spending its time on) and #157989 (the same source-capture machinery also rewrites GBs per start — the capture directory is per plugin *workspace*, and this issue is about the CPU cost of the per-instance module registry, not the I/O).

### Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.6 (eb377ac)**, npm global install, Windows 11 x64 (10.0.26200), Node **v24.19.0**
- 23 enabled plugins; the three heavy channels: `@openclaw/feishu` 2026.9.6, `@dingtalk-real-ai/dingtalk-connector` 0.8.26, `@tencent-weixin/openclaw-weixin` 2.4.6 (all installed via npm into `<stateDir>/npm/projects/...`)
- Gateway started with `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` set and `--max-old-space-size=8192`

### Steps to reproduce

1. Install the three plugins above into an npm-based install and start the Gateway with `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_STARTUP_TRACE=1`.
2. Read the `startup trace: plugins.gateway-load.plugin.<id> ... loadMs= registerMs= loadAndRegisterMs=` lines.
3. In a separate cold Node process, `import()` the plugin's entry module (e.g. `@openclaw/feishu/dist/index.js` → `loadChannelPlugin()` → `dist/channel-plugin-api.js`) and time it.
4. Repeat step 3 after first `require()`-ing the `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` subpaths that the plugin imports.

### Expected behavior

An installed, unchanged plugin's module graph should be compiled once per process (or once per build) and reused across plugin instances, so that enabling N channel plugins costs roughly the compile of the union of the graphs, not N × (shared graph + own graph).

### Actual behavior

**1. Gateway-side per-plugin cost (2026.9.6 eb377ac, Windows)**

| plugin | `loadMs` | `registerMs` | `loadAndRegisterMs` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `feishu` | 18,843.0 | 21,805.6 | **40,649.0** |
| `dingtalk-connector` | 12,112.8 | 10.1 | **12,123.0** |
| `openclaw-weixin` | 4,625.3 | 2.5 | **4,627.9** |
| (next 16 plugins combined) | — | — | **~0.6 s** |

`plugins.runtime-post-bind` = **59,959.9 ms**, `loadedPluginCount=23`. The phase's own liveness line says the main thread was saturated while it ran:

```
liveness warning: reasons=event_loop_delay,event_loop_utilization,cpu interval=61s degradedFor=62s
  eventLoopDelayP99Ms=60196.7 eventLoopDelayMaxMs=60196.7 eventLoopUtilization=0.999 cpuCoreRatio=0.914
  active=0 waiting=0 queued=0 phase=sidecars.control-ui-assets
```

**2. Cold-process cost of one plugin entry, measured outside the Gateway (5 runs each, min/median/max)**

| what was imported | wall time |
|---|---|
| `@openclaw/feishu/dist/channel-plugin-api.js` (a 92-byte file that re-exports one `.setup/channel-*.mjs`) | **7,212 / 7,303 / 7,497 ms** (one run during an active session: 13,186 ms) |
| `@tencent-weixin/openclaw-weixin/dist/index.js` | **4,932 / 4,968 / 5,040 ms** |
| `@dingtalk-real-ai/dingtalk-connector/dist/index.mjs` | ~835 ms (only 66 modules) |
| third-party SDK alone: `@larksuiteoapi/node-sdk` / `axios` / `dingtalk-stream` / `zod` | **264 / 136 / 159 / 118 ms** |

Variance is small (weixin: 4,932–5,040 ms over 5 runs), so this is deterministic compile cost, not scheduling noise.

**3. Where inside weixin's 5 s it goes — cumulative cost of the SDK subpaths it imports**

| subpath (in import order) | cumulative |
|---|---|
| `openclaw/plugin-sdk/account-id` | 11 ms |
| `+ channel-config-schema` | 733 ms |
| `+ channel-runtime` | 1,564 ms |
| `+ command-auth` | 2,659 ms |
| `+ config-runtime` | 2,770 ms |
| `+ hook-runtime`, `infra-runtime`, `plugin-runtime` | ~5,400 ms |

The plugin's own entry is 716 bytes and imports 4 local files; the whole 5 s is the SDK graph behind it. (`feishu` imports 20 distinct `openclaw/plugin-sdk/*` subpaths.)

**4. Control: warm the SDK graph, and the same import is 20x cheaper**

| case | cold | after warming only the plugin-sdk subpaths |
|---|---|---|
| weixin `dist/index.js` | 4,968 ms | **224 ms** (285 modules) |
| dingtalk `dist/index.mjs` | 835 ms | **448 ms** |
| feishu `dist/channel-plugin-api.js` | 7,303 ms | **3,121 ms** (still loaded 222 more modules beyond the 19 subpaths that were statically enumerable) |

**5. CPU profile of one such import** (`--cpu-prof`, weixin `dist/src/config/config-schema.js`, 6,015 ms sampled, 279 modules)

| self time | frame |
|---|---|
| 2,710.5 ms | `ModuleWrap` (ESM wrapping/compile) |
| 357.5 ms | `internalModuleStat` |
| 321.0 ms | `compileSourceTextModule` |
| 261.6 ms | `compileFunctionForCJSLoader` |
| ~1,300 ms | file I/O (`open` 153 / `read` 108 / `lstat` 115 / `realpathSync` 121 / `fstat` 54 / `readFileUtf8` 50) |
| 90.3 / 198.8 / 323.9 ms | `esm/module_job` / `esm/loader` / `esm/utils` |
| 63.7 ms | GC |

**6. `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` does not help this path** (2 controlled pairs, same module): 2,421 / 2,293 ms without the cache vs 2,609 (populate) / 5,021 ms (hit) with it. The 16 MB cache dir (4,332 files) is written but the compile cost stays — i.e. the cost is resolve + read + compile + instantiate of the graph, not V8 code-cache territory.

### Hypothesis (not proven)

The plugin instance isolation introduced with source capture gives each plugin its own module registry, so the *shared* SDK graph is compiled again for each instance instead of being reused process-wide. Consistent with the numbers: in one plain Node process the SDK graph is shared (`require.cache`), and weixin costs 224 ms after feishu warmed it, while in the Gateway the second and third heavy channel plugin still cost 12.1 s and 4.6 s. A build-time diagnostic would settle it.

### Available instrumentation for maintainers

`plugin.load-profile` already exists: `OPENCLAW_DIAGNOSTICS=plugin.load-profile` (or `diagnostics.flags`) makes `src/plugins/plugin-load-profile.ts` emit one stderr line per phase:

```
[plugin-load-profile] phase=bundled-register:loadChannelPlugin  plugin=feishu elapsedMs=… source=…
[plugin-load-profile] phase=bundled-entry-module-load elapsedMs=13186.6 sourceLoaderCreateMs=0.0 sourceLoaderCallMs=0.0 source=…/dist/channel-plugin-api.js
```

`bundled-register:*` (`loadChannelPlugin` / `registerChannel` / `setChannelRuntime` / `registerFull` / `registerCapabilities`) and `bundled-entry-module-load` give exactly the per-plugin split this report infers, and `sourceLoaderCallMs=0` tells you the native-require path was taken rather than the source-transform loader. We verified the flag works in a standalone process; we have not yet captured a Gateway boot with it (that requires enabling it and restarting, which we will do next and attach here).

One data point from that standalone harness: with the plugin's modules already warm, the entire `register(registrationMode="full")` call took **43 ms** — so feishu's Gateway-side `registerMs=21,805.6` looks like further *module loads* inside the same phase (its `registerFull` synchronously loads six tool modules: doc / chat / wiki / drive / perm / bitable), not registration logic.

### Honest limits

- All per-module timings are from the **reported release (2026.9.6 eb377ac)**, measured in standalone Node processes on this host, not from current main. The Gateway-side numbers (table 1) are from the Gateway's own startup trace on the same release.
- The "per-instance registry defeats sharing" explanation is a **hypothesis**; the per-plugin splits needed to confirm it require the `plugin.load-profile` run described above.
- The 13,186 ms outlier for the same feishu module was measured while the Gateway was serving a session; all other runs were on a quiet host.

issues.body:
## Summary

Self-hosted gateway (2026.9.6, npm latest; macOS arm64, Node 24.19.0) wedged under heavy Control-UI/webchat use of one agent whose SQLite session store is ~4.3 GB: one core pegged at 100%, TCP accepts but HTTP never answers (curl connects, 0 bytes, times out), ~50 threads idle in `kevent`. A watchdog restarted it (~13 min outage). Retention is NOT the issue — the store is at steady state under `session.maintenance` caps (470 unarchived < 500 maxEntries, disk under the 8 GiB high-water mark).

## Evidence 1 — synchronous main-thread SQLite in the serving process

The gateway's own slow-transaction logs during boot (`async:false, isMainThread:true, threadId 0, thresholdMs 1000`):

- `sqlite/transaction` `media-persistence-detection` elapsedMs **4332**
- `state/agent-db` admission (`admissionMode: "sync"`) validation **2907 ms**, of which `integrityCheckSyncMs` 2893
- even the `openclaw memory reset` CLI logged a **2086 ms** sync main-thread hold

## Evidence 2 — wedge stack samples: JS churn, not sqlite

macOS `sample` of the wedged process (two captures, seconds apart):

- ALL hot frames on `com.apple.main-thread` (219 and 643 hot frames respectively; every other thread idle)
- V8 Scavenger (young-gen GC) storms — 618 frame lines in one capture — plus `simdutf convert_latin1_to_utf8`, `__findenv_locked` (getenv lock) contention, and `Runtime_String` frames
- **ZERO sqlite3/better-sqlite3 C frames in either capture** → the event loop is busy in JS deserialization/allocation churn around store reads, not inside the sqlite engine

## Evidence 3 — worker modules exist but these paths don't use them

The dist ships `infra/sqlite-store.worker.js`, `infra/sqlite-readonly-location.worker.js` (a readonly child does run in production), and `state/openclaw-state-read.worker.js` — yet the write-path transactions and the boot integrity gate run synchronously on the main thread of the same process that serves HTTP/WebSocket.

## Reproduction context

- Agent store: ~4.3 GB, 2,782 sessions, 183k `transcript_events`, append-only design, WAL + `auto_vacuum=incremental`, `quick_check ok`
- Trigger window: ~9 min of heavy dashboard/webchat use (session listing, `chat.history` fetches, embedded subagent runs)
- A clean safe-restart on the same DB reaches `http server listening` in ~38 s, so this is not cold-cache IO
- Offline VACUUM of a copy changes warm-query timings by ~0 — file bloat is not the driver

Possibly related but distinct: #144460 (main thread in futex wait = blocked syscall; this report is a CPU-busy loop).

## Ask

Move and/or bound agent-store work off the serving thread — e.g. route the write path and boot integrity gate through the existing worker modules, and bound/paginate large reads — or add an event-loop-lag circuit breaker so a busy loop can't silently starve `/health`.

Happy to share the full `sample` captures and log excerpts.

issues.body:
## Summary

Provide a supported CLI messaging mode for scripts launched by an agent's `exec` tool that preserves the originating agent/session attribution.

## Problem to solve

[PR #150499](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/150499) intentionally rejects Gateway-backed operator message commands from `OPENCLAW_SHELL=exec` because they cannot preserve inter-session provenance. Existing script-based handoffs now fail with:

> Gateway agent from agent exec would lose inter-session attribution.

A concrete use case is a top-level heartbeat agent running an existing shell/Python helper to hand follow-up work to another agent session. The helper encapsulates the target, payload preparation and response handling, and may also be invoked by an ordinary system scheduler. This is not necessarily a spawned child's completion report.

The suggested replacement, calling `sessions_send` from the model's tool interface, requires moving handoff orchestration out of the script and changing its callers. A CLI should also be able to perform this handoff with explicit structured attribution.

## Proposed solution

Add an explicit attributed mode to the existing CLI messaging surface, or a dedicated CLI subcommand, backed by the existing agent-to-agent messaging/admission implementation.

The originating context should be supplied or validated by the runtime, rather than inferred from a message prefix or accepted solely from a caller-selected agent ID. The exact mechanism can reuse an existing context bridge or a scoped local capability; this request does not prescribe a new credential system.

Expected behavior:

- A helper launched through agent `exec` can send to an authorized peer session with `OPENCLAW_SHELL=exec` left intact.
- The receiving session, prompt envelope and history retain structured agent-origin provenance and the correct source session, rather than classifying the handoff as fresh operator input.
- The operation retains the originating run's applicable permissions and messaging restrictions.
- The attributed mode has explicit, documented queue/steering, timeout and reply-delivery semantics. The introducing PR notes that silently translating an operator call would change those semantics; an explicit mode lets scripts opt into the appropriate contract.
- Ordinary human-terminal and system-scheduler CLI behavior remains available. Existing helpers can adopt the new mode without moving their orchestration into model prompts.

## Alternatives considered

- Use the native `sessions_send` tool: appropriate for model-driven coordination, but not a script-callable replacement for existing helpers.
- Add an agent-origin prefix to the payload: provides readable context, but not structured runtime provenance.
- Expose only an agent/session environment variable: useful for correlation, but not by itself a validated messaging path.

## Impact

Affected: installations with script-based peer handoffs launched by top-level agents.

Frequency: every affected agent-exec handoff under the new guard.

Consequence: working automation stops at dispatch and requires caller/workflow changes even when the operator is willing to adapt the helper to carry attribution. A supported CLI path would let these installations retain their script interfaces.

## Evidence/examples

- Observed on OpenClaw source build `2026.9.6`, examined at `56376753f`.
- [Issue #150467](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/150467) establishes the structured-provenance problem this feature should preserve the fix for.
- Related: [#137299](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/137299) requests calling-agent identity for exec children. This proposal asks for an end-to-end attributed CLI messaging capability, not just an identity marker.

## Do you plan to open a PR for this?

No, proposing the idea only.

issues.body:
# Duplicate Telegram delivery of agent reply via wrong (default) account after session context reset

## Version

OpenClaw 2026.7.1-beta.6 (a783a2b), single gateway process, Linux, Node 22.

## Setup

- Multiple Telegram bot accounts configured (`default`, `steve-rogers`, and several others), each with a binding: `{"agentId": "steve-rogers", "match": {"channel": "telegram", "accountId": "steve-rogers"}}`.
- The `steve-rogers` agent has its own workspace and edits its own `MEMORY.md` mid-turn.
- The agent's session was reset on Sep 27 (reset artifact `.jsonl.reset.2026-09-27T05-46-53.506Z`); after the reset the session key for the same Telegram direct chat **lost its account segment**:
  - before: `agent:steve-rogers:telegram:steve-rogers:direct:1314589251`
  - after: `agent:steve-rogers:telegram:direct:1314589251`

## What happened

The user messaged the `steve-rogers` bot. The agent's turn completed normally (reply text emitted mid-turn alongside a tool call, turn ended with NO_REPLY). The user then received **the same reply text twice, ~75 seconds apart** — and the second copy was sent by the **default account's bot**, not the agent's own bot.

## Timeline (UTC, gateway journal)

```
01:30:49  [telegram] Inbound message telegram:1314589251 -> @mok_steve_bot (direct, 25 chars)
01:31:21  model call #2 completes; turn ends with NO_REPLY
01:31:22  visible reply appended to the agent session jsonl (first delivery, see note below)
01:32:36  [agents/harness] Codex agent harness session reset hook failed   <-- src/agents/harness/registry.ts:75
01:32:37  [telegram] sendMessage ok chat=1314589251 message=6784           <-- second delivery
01:32:52  [telegram] Inbound message telegram:1314589251 -> @mok_jarvis_bot (direct)  message_id=6785
```

Note: no API-call log exists for the first delivery — since the Sep 27 session reset, sends for this agent no longer log `outbound send ok accountId=steve-rogers ...` (last such line was Sep 27 13:00:39, messageId=94), while replies still reach the user. The only logged API call is the 01:32:37 one.

## Evidence the second copy went through the default account

- The second send logs in the low-level format without any account: `[telegram] sendMessage ok chat=1314589251 message=6784` (`extensions/telegram/src/bot/delivery.send.ts:170`).
- The user's next message **to the default account's bot** is `message_id=6785` — immediately consecutive with 6784 in that chat. The `steve-rogers` bot's chat is at message id ~94 (its last account-tagged send), so 6784 cannot belong to that chat; per-chat id sequences are independent.

## Suspected mechanism

1. The agent edited its own workspace `MEMORY.md` during the turn, invalidating the session context (bootstrap file change) → session reset flow ran ~75s after turn completion.
2. Something in the reset/re-validation path **re-flushed the already-delivered visible reply** (second API call at 01:32:37, 1s after the reset-hook log line).
3. The re-flush resolved the outbound Telegram account from context that **no longer carries the account binding** (consistent with the account segment having been dropped from the session key), so it fell back to the `default` account and sent the reply from the wrong bot.
4. The message-id dedupe mentioned in `src/auto-reply/reply/queue/enqueue.ts` ("shared across bundled chunks so redeliveries ...") apparently does not cover this path.

## Expected behavior

- A reply that was already delivered should not be re-sent after a session context reset (dedupe by delivery/turn identity).
- Outbound account selection for an agent's reply should come from the inbound envelope / binding, so a session key that lost its account segment cannot cause a reply to be sent from another bot's account.

## Impact

User-visible duplicate messages from the wrong bot identity; also silently breaks per-account send logging after a session reset. Observed once so far; an identical earlier turn did not duplicate (the reset-hook event did not fire then), which matches the mechanism above.

## What shows today

In the Control UI sidebar, every row in the top block of pages (Agents, Dashboards, Systems, Automations, Plugins, plugin pages and pinned sessions) has a grip button at its trailing edge. With a mouse it appears when the row is hovered or active ("Reorder Agents", opening a **Move up** / **Move down** menu); on touch screens it is always visible. Even when it is invisible, the row keeps a 24px slot for it, so the page link and its highlight stop 24px short of the sidebar edge.

## Why it is not needed for pointer users

These rows already reorder by dragging, which is the obvious gesture for mouse and touch users. The grip adds a second, less direct control for the same thing and costs horizontal space in a sidebar that is already narrow.

Keyboard and screen-reader users cannot drag, so the **Reorder** menu must stay available to them: reachable with Tab, announced as "Reorder <page>", and moving the entry with **Move up** / **Move down** as today. The grip on stored session-section headers is a separate control and is not part of this issue.

issues.body:
### Summary
Let coordinator agents maintain their own Markdown memory through an independently grantable capability, without general filesystem write/edit or exec access.

### Problem to solve
A coordinator can be intentionally restricted to planning and delegation yet still need to retain decisions and preferences. Granting workspace-wide writes also exposes unrelated files; prompt instructions alone are not an enforced boundary. Keeping all writes disabled makes routine memory maintenance depend on another actor.

### Proposed solution
Provide a narrowly scoped capability for eligible `MEMORY.md` and `memory/*.md` targets within the agent's own workspace, preserving file-backed memory.

Desired constraints:
- Trusted runtime path enforcement, including traversal/symlink escape handling; no arbitrary files, prompt files, or configuration writes.
- Independent admission from general write/edit/exec tools.
- Read-before-edit and concurrency/conflict guards for any updates.
- Integration with memory provenance and indexing rather than a parallel untracked writer.

Append-only versus bounded edits is an open design choice, as is whether this belongs in a plugin or a core capability. These are requirements to discuss, not claimed security guarantees.

### Alternatives considered
Delegate writes to a permitted agent or human; grant broad writes; switch to LanceDB. These either add coordination, broaden access, or change the Markdown storage model.

### Impact
Affected: restricted multi-agent coordinators. Workflow friction whenever durable notes need updating; consequences are manual handoffs or overly broad permissions. No measured frequency or performance claims.

### Evidence/examples
Related design discussion: #116499. Prior art: #21003, closed for inactivity, not an explicit rejection of memory tools.

### Do you plan to open a PR for this?
No, proposing the idea only

### Additional information
This is a concrete use-case/interest check, not a claim of no prior work or a replacement for #116499. Do others need this? Would maintainers prefer consolidating this use case there?

On 2026.9.6, a guarded Skill Workshop apply from an agent-to-agent continuation fails at `plugin.approval.request` with `missing scope: operator.approvals`, but the agent receives `Plugin approval required (gateway unavailable)` while the Gateway is healthy.

The exact provenance/scope conditions needed to reproduce on another installation have not been isolated.

The error presented to the agent should distinguish an authorization rejection from a transport outage, consistent with the actual Gateway error. If this continuation is ineligible to request approval, provide an actionable supported operator handoff. If eligible, route the request to the operator without granting the agent approval-resolution authority.

The tool returned `Plugin approval required (gateway unavailable)`. The Gateway log instead recorded `GatewayClientRequestError: missing scope: operator.approvals`. Gateway connectivity was healthy. `openclaw approvals pending --json` returned an empty list; that list alone is not proof of plugin approval absence, but the logged request rejection establishes the earlier failure. The proposal remained pending and live skill files were unchanged.

2026.9.6 (eb377ac)

## Operating system
macOS 27.0, Apple Silicon

## Install method
Global npm package

## Model
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

## Provider / routing chain
NOT_ENOUGH_INFO

Sanitized error text from the incident:
```text
plugin approval gateway request failed
GatewayClientRequestError: missing scope: operator.approvals
Plugin approval required (gateway unavailable)
```

Installed bundle inspection:
- `agent-tools.before-tool-call-D6M7yTR3.mjs:989`: calls `plugin.approval.request`.

- 14:40:07–14:40:11 the queued run (`runId 9cedc381…`) started and died: `embedded run agent end … isError=true … rawError=Session transcript anchor was not returned: 6bcc98d5-…` ×3 (`[empty-error-retry] … resubmitting attempt=2/3, 3/3`), `failover decision=fallback_model … next=none`, then `Embedded agent failed before reply: Failed to persist terminal assistant error: session rebound for sessionKey: agent:main:main`, `message dispatch completed … outcome=error duration=561573ms`.
- The user received "⚠️ Something went wrong while processing your request. Please try again, or use /new to start a fresh session." No alert anywhere; the user turn IS persisted in the transcript (14:32:14), so a later run can still see it.

**Reading:** the queued run captured its transcript anchor (the parent event id to append after) at dispatch time; the safeguard compaction that ran while it waited finalized a new artifact and rebound the session (`lifecycleRevision`), so the anchor no longer exists when the run finally executes. Retrying the same request 3× cannot help (same stale anchor); model failover is irrelevant (`reason=unknown`).

**Expected:** a run admitted after a compaction/rebind should re-resolve its anchor to the current transcript head (or the compaction should be deferred while runs are queued for that session); the failure should be classified as a session error, not a model failover, and surfaced to operators.

**Repro:** long active run on a session + a queued inbound message + `maxActiveTranscriptBytes` small enough that a safeguard compaction lands during the wait.

_Filed from a production single-operator deployment; happy to provide redacted logs or test a patch._

### Beta release blocker

### Summary

Environment

OpenClaw: 2026.9.7 (c074824)

Node.js: v24.21.0

OS: Linux x86_64

Kernel:
Linux [vps].de 5.2.0 #1 SMP Mon Sep 30 15:36:27 MSK 2024 x86_64 GNU/Linux

Gateway: system-wide systemd service

Service file: /etc/systemd/system/openclaw.service

Gateway stopped during all migration/repair attempts

OPENCLAW_SERVICE_REPAIR_POLICY=external

Summary

After upgrading to OpenClaw 2026.9.7, two agent databases require session-identity migration:

~/.openclaw/agents/main/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite

~/.openclaw/agents/openclaw/agent/openclaw-agent.sqlite

Both use schema version 19.

Running openclaw doctor --fix while the Gateway is completely stopped reproducibly damages the existing shared-state database:

~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

The command creates its normal pre-migration backups, then aborts with:

Doctor could not complete maintenance.
Check the reported service state and resolve the failure.
Existing shared-state database generation changed:
/home/superadmin/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

After the failed repair, the live openclaw.sqlite has been observed as a 0-byte file.

Restoring the shared-state database from the automatically generated pre-migration backup makes read-only OpenClaw commands work again.



### Steps to reproduce

Reproduction

Stop the Gateway completely:

sudo systemctl stop openclaw.service
ps -ef | grep '[o]penclaw'

No OpenClaw process remains.

Verify the restored shared-state DB:

file ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

Result:

SQLite 3.x database, user version 19, ...

Current state:

size=7892992

Read-only doctor succeeds:

OPENCLAW_SERVICE_REPAIR_POLICY=external \
openclaw doctor --lint --json

The remaining relevant findings are only that the two agent databases use schema version 19 and require doctor --fix.

Session SQLite inspection also confirms both agent databases are healthy:

openclaw doctor \
  --session-sqlite inspect \
  --session-sqlite-all-agents \
  --json

Results:

main

DB size: 81571840

integrityCheck: "ok"

11 SQLite session entries

no issues

openclaw

DB size: 602112

integrityCheck: "ok"

no issues

Run the requested repair:

OPENCLAW_SERVICE_REPAIR_POLICY=external \
openclaw doctor --fix

Doctor creates pre-migration backups and then exits with:

Existing shared-state database generation changed:
/home/superadmin/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

After a failed run, the live shared-state DB has been observed as:

-rw------- ... openclaw.sqlite

with size:

0 bytes

No process has the DB/WAL/SHM files open according to lsof.

Recovery

Restoring the automatically generated pre-migration backup restores normal read-only access:

cp \
  ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite.pre-startup-migration-<uuid>.bak \
  ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

After restoration:

file ~/.openclaw/state/openclaw.sqlite

again reports:

SQLite 3.x database, user version 19

and:

OPENCLAW_SERVICE_REPAIR_POLICY=external \
openclaw doctor --lint --json

works again without the generation changed error.

Current shared-state file

dev=1533064801
inode=2758105
birth=-
size=7892992
mtime=2026-09-30 22:30:02.630829665 +0000
ctime=2026-09-30 22:30:02.630829665 +0000

Relevant code path

The failure appears to originate from the existing shared-state generation guard in the 2026.9.7 build:

if (
  !current.isFile() ||
  current.dev !== original.dev ||
  current.ino !== original.ino ||
  current.birthtimeNs !== original.birthtimeNs
) {

doctor --fix should migrate the agent databases while preserving the existing healthy shared-state database.

If a migration cannot safely proceed, it should abort without modifying or truncating the canonical openclaw.sqlite.

Actual behavior

doctor --fix reproducibly aborts with:

Existing shared-state database generation changed

No OpenClaw process remains.

Read-only doctor works after restoring the backup.

Both agent DBs pass SQLite integrity inspection.

The issue is reproducible.

Downgrading is not a viable workaround because the restored state DB already uses schema version 19.

Manual schema editing has not been attempted.

The automatically generated pre-migration backups successfully preserve the original data.

This looks like a data-loss-risk issue in the 2026.9.7 repair/migration path.

Update should have run through without any errors and resulting in an operataional updated OpenClaw instance.

openclaw System is down.

issues.body:
**Environment**
- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (build eb377ac), Windows 10, Node 24.21.0
- Agent backend: `claude-cli` (Claude Code CLI, subscription login), one agent, one gateway on loopback
- A third-party plugin exposes tools to the CLI backend through the process-owned MCP loopback server; one tool declares an approval requirement (`plugin.approval.request`)
- Clients: the Control UI (browser webchat) and the Companion app, both paired as operator devices

**Summary**
On the `claude-cli` backend, plugin tools are served by an MCP loopback server that is started lazily during the first CLI turn after gateway start. The server keeps the gateway request scope of that first turn. When a tool later triggers `plugin.approval.request`, the in-process dispatch checks `hasCurrentClientAuthority()` on that stored scope. As soon as the WebSocket connection of that first client is gone (page reload or navigation in the Control UI, Companion restart), every subsequent plugin approval request fails with

```
[agents/tools] plugin approval gateway request failed; blocking tool call:
Error: Gateway client authority closed before dispatching plugin.approval.request.
```

and stays failed until the gateway process is restarted. Approval-gated plugin tools are therefore fail-closed for the rest of the gateway lifetime, even though the requester of the new turn is an authenticated, currently connected operator.

**Reproduction (three controlled runs, same day)**
1. Start the gateway. Connect the Companion app only and send a plain message. The first CLI turn starts the loopback server (`server/discover`, `initialize`, `tools/list` visible with the loopback debug flag).
2. From the same Companion window ask for the approval-gated tool while no Control UI is open: the request fails early with `Plugin approval unavailable, no approval route` (the node client is not treated as an approval surface). No card.
3. Open the Control UI, keep the Companion connected, ask again: the approval card appears in the Control UI, `allow-once` runs the tool. Works.
4. Quit and relaunch the Companion (its WebSocket is replaced), keep the Control UI open, ask again: no card, the error above is logged, the tool is blocked. This state persists.
5. Restart the gateway, repeat step 1 from the Companion, then step 3: works again. The behaviour is deterministic with respect to which connection made the first CLI turn.
6. Variant: when the first CLI turn is made from the Control UI, a single page reload is enough to reach the failed state.

**Code pointers (dist, 2026.9.6)**
- `prepare.runtime-*.mjs` (loopback start during the first CLI turn's prepare) → `mcp-http-*.mjs` (server keeps the creating request scope)
- `gateway-request-scope-*.mjs`: "authenticated Gateway caller and authority stay attached"
- `device-revocation-*.mjs`: `isCurrent = isRevocationCurrent() && hasCurrentClientAuthority()` — authority is tied to the connection
- `server-plugin-in-process-dispatch-*.mjs`: throws `Gateway client authority closed before dispatching plugin.approval.request.` when `hasCurrentClientAuthority?.() === false`

**Expected behaviour**
The approval dispatch should verify the authority of the client that owns the current turn (the requester of the tool call), or a per-turn scope handed to the loopback call, and keep rejecting when that requester's authority is closed, revoked or not an operator. It should not depend on the liveness of whichever connection happened to trigger the loopback server's lazy start. Fail-closed behaviour for an unauthorised or disconnected requester must remain.

**Impact**
Any plugin that relies on the official approval flow becomes unusable on the `claude-cli` backend after a routine client reconnect, with no recovery short of a gateway restart. Operators may mistake the error for a plugin defect.

**Workaround in use**
Restart the gateway, make the first CLI turn from the longest-lived client, keep a Control UI tab open as the approval surface. No configuration or code bypass is applied.

**Related issues (checked, not duplicates)**
- #156135 — loopback MCP server lazy start on the `claude-cli` backend (asks how to avoid starting it; this report is about the request scope it keeps)
- #128779 — plugin approval surface missing for ACP shell prompts in Slack (different surface; mentions fail-closed on gateway restart)

issues.body:
### Bug type

Behavior bug (incorrect output/state without crash)

### Beta release blocker

No

### Summary

A message sent from the Control UI composer while a reply is running is accepted by the Gateway, but within about two seconds the Control UI's stored outbox row flips from `sending` to `waiting-reconnect` on a socket that never closed, so the message shows "Waiting for reconnect" and messages queued behind it can sit in `waiting-idle` without being attempted.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open the Control UI in a plain browser (reproduced in headless Chromium driven by playwright-core, no extension or injected script).
2. Send a prompt that produces a long reply.
3. While it is replying, send a second message, then a third.
4. Read `sessionStorage["openclaw.control.chatComposer.v4:<gateway>"]`, or look at the queued rows.

Minimal reproduction without a Gateway: the two regression tests in the linked PR write the outbox twice from the same page instance, as the live page does on its next draft or send. On current `main` (dfb6474c538):

```
× chat composer persistence > keeps a sending row in flight when the same page rewrites the outbox
  expected ["in-flight","sending"], received ["in-flight","waiting-reconnect"]
× chat composer persistence > keeps a submitting row in flight when the same page rewrites the outbox
  received ["in-flight","waiting-idle"]
Tests  2 failed | 60 passed (62)
```

### Expected behavior

The second message stays `sending` until the Gateway's receipt retires it, and no reconnect state appears without a reconnect. The Control UI's own disconnect handling (`markQueuedChatSendsWaitingForReconnect`) is the path meant to move an in-flight row to `waiting-reconnect`.

### Actual behavior

The row is stored as `waiting-reconnect` with `sendAttempts: 1` about two seconds after the `chat.send` ack, with zero WebSocket closes. The row then shows "Waiting for reconnect" / "Reconnected before delivery was confirmed. Check the conversation, retry only if your message didn't arrive." for a message the Gateway already has. In the browser run the third message was stored `waiting-idle`, `sendAttempts: 0`, while the second sat in `waiting-reconnect`.

Cause: `normalizeStoredQueueItem` in `ui/src/lib/chat/outbox-store-codec.ts` maps `sending` to `waiting-reconnect` and `submitting` to `waiting-idle`. That is the right replay rule after a reload, but the codec runs on every write (`serializeQueueItem` in `ui/src/pages/chat/composer-queue-serialization.ts`) and every read (`readStoredOutboxStore`), so a live page downgrades its own in-flight send the next time the outbox is written. The existing test "normalizes sending before durable replay" encodes the downgrade within a single page instance, which is why no test tripped.

### OpenClaw version

2026.9.6 (eb377ac); still present on `main` at dfb6474c538

### Operating system

Gateway on Linux (containerized); browser client on macOS

### Install method

Docker

### Model

Not model-dependent (Control UI outbox state); observed with an Anthropic model

### Provider / routing chain

openclaw -> anthropic (direct provider)

### Logs

WebSocket frames from the browser page (credentials redacted), for the second message:

- `chat.send` acked `status: "started"` in 36 ms.
- The next `chat.history` listed it in `pendingInputs` with `state: "queued"` and `runId` equal to the send id.
- The stored row read `waiting-reconnect` at the next sample.
- The transcript later carried it once, with `idempotencyKey: "<send id>:user"`.
- No `close` event on the page socket at any point.

### Impact and severity

Any user who types while a reply is running can see a false reconnect warning on a delivered message and have later queued messages held until something else triggers a drain. Also reproduced in a desktop shell that embeds the same Control UI.

issues.body:
### Summary
On this Windows machine the update flow fails repeatedly, and every failure emits a user-visible notice. Five failure records accumulated in ~2 days. Three distinct failure modes were observed on the same box.

---
#### 1) `managed-service-preflight` — updater runs inside the gateway process tree
```
⚠️ OpenClaw update failed: managed-service-preflight.
Phases: requested (22.91s) → staging (209ms) → validating (969.9s) → activating (18.85s)
Failed: activating
Failing check managed-service-preflight: This command is running inside the gateway
process tree (gateway PID <pid>).
```
The updater is spawned as a descendant of the gateway, so activation is refused. Refusing may be correct, but the auto-update path keeps producing this instead of handing the run to the managed helper.

#### 2) `runtime-verification-failed` — snapshot path contains an unexpanded env var
```
Failed: candidate snapshot — Exit code: 1;  directory, mkdir
'~\AppData\Local\Temp\openclaw-update-canary-XXXXXX\?\$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR\agents\main\agent' (13495ms)
```
Note the literal `$OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and the `\?\` prefix. The canary/snapshot copy cannot create the agent dir, so the run degrades to "repairing" and then fails.

#### 3) `reconcile:abandoned` / `inactive-driver-dead` after a gateway restart
```
⚠️ OpenClaw update failed: abandoned. Phases: requested (1891.62s). Failed: requested.
Failed: reconcile:abandoned — inactive-driver-dead.
Recorded verification: gateway booted; service running.
```
An update queued at the same moment as a gateway restart sat in `requested` for ~31 minutes until the reconciler abandoned it because its driver process was gone (killed by the same restart). The user gets a failure notice for a run that was already superseded.

---
#### Related: validation is very slow and the inspection window is exhausted
```
Phases: requested (22.91s) → staging (209ms) → validating (969.9s) → activating (18.85s)
Warning: Doctor lint inspection deferred until after activation: 1 agent scopes need a 2000ms
inspection allowance, with 0ms remaining in the validation inspection window (validation-ledger).
```
Validating took ~16 minutes here (SQLite family ≈419 MiB + ~160 MiB of plugin files; snapshot needs ≈2.1 GiB scratch). The lint allowance was exhausted, so repairs were deferred post-activation.

### Workaround currently in use
`update.auto.enabled` was set to `false` to stop the recurring failed-update notices; updates are triggered manually via `/update`.

### Suggestions
- Always hand auto-update runs to the managed helper (never launch inside the gateway process tree), or detect the condition before spending ~17 minutes staging/validating.
- Fix snapshot path construction on Windows (expand `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`; drop the literal `\?\`).
- Treat `reconcile:abandoned` after a restart as a quiet log entry rather than a user-facing failure notice.
- Make the validation inspection budget adaptive, or report an exhausted window as info instead of a deferred-repair warning.

### Environment
- OpenClaw 2026.9.6 (eb377ac) — also reproduced on 2026.9.5
- Windows 10.0.26200 x64, node v24.18.0, PowerShell 5.1
- Gateway managed by a Windows Scheduled Task via a generated `gateway.vbs` hidden WScript wrapper
- Install: npm global (`%APPDATA%\npm\node_modules\openclaw`)
