- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.title: [Feature]: Add Microsoft MXC sandbox backend support
issues.body:
### Summary

Add Microsoft eXecution Container (MXC) as an explicitly selectable sandbox backend (`security.sandbox.backend = "mxc"`), with native Windows support as the initial target.

### Problem statement

ZeroClaw currently exposes `auto`, `landlock`, `firejail`, `bubblewrap`, `docker`, `sandboxexec`, and `none` in `SandboxBackend`. Its native OS sandbox choices are primarily Linux and macOS oriented; Docker requires a container runtime. A native Windows MXC option would provide another containment path for agent tool execution without requiring Docker.

Microsoft's MXC provides typed SDKs, including Rust, and a common containment model across platform-specific backends. OpenAI Codex already contains a native Windows MXC integration, providing a useful implementation reference.

### Proposed solution

- Add an opt-in `mxc` sandbox selection through the existing sandbox configuration and factory.
- Scope the first implementation to native Windows execution, subject to maintainer assessment. Evaluate Linux/macOS integration separately rather than assuming equivalent enforcement across MXC backends.
- Evaluate the Rust `mxc-sdk` integration and pin the selected dependency revision/version. Keep platform-specific dependencies and build costs isolated.
- Translate the effective ZeroClaw filesystem and network policy into MXC requests. Existing configuration and runtime policy remain the source of truth; do not introduce a separate MXC permission store or long-lived snapshots of mutable policy.
- Probe actual runtime capabilities before execution. Reject unsupported requested restrictions and unavailable explicitly selected MXC configurations with actionable diagnostics; do not silently execute with weaker isolation.
- Preserve command arguments, working directory, environment, standard I/O, exit status, timeout, and cancellation semantics. Own the native policy/container for the full workload lifetime and define descendant-process cleanup behavior.
- Report requested and effective sandbox selection in the existing security status surfaces and document prerequisites and known limitations.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Changing the default backend or automatic selection order in the initial release.
- Implementing every MXC backend, a new container orchestration layer, or a separate policy language.
- Relaxing approval, allowlist, filesystem, or network boundaries to make a command work.
- Assuming VM-level isolation for all MXC modes: MXC is an integration layer over backends with different security properties.

### Alternatives considered

| Option | Current role / platform | Comparison with the requested MXC integration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Landlock | Existing Linux kernel sandbox | Useful Linux-native enforcement; does not supply native Windows containment. |
| Firejail / Bubblewrap | Existing Linux sandbox choices | Remain useful Linux options. MXC itself can use Bubblewrap on Linux, so adopting MXC there would not automatically create a stronger boundary. |
| sandbox-exec / Seatbelt | Existing macOS sandbox | Remains the macOS-native option. MXC also lists Seatbelt for macOS; evaluate any added value separately. |
| Docker | Existing container isolation | Useful when a container runtime is available; MXC offers a native Windows integration path with different deployment and lifecycle requirements. |
| Application-layer-only execution | Existing `none` choice | Does not add an OS containment boundary. It should not be an implicit fallback for an explicit MXC request. |
| External MXC wrapper | Possible integration outside ZeroClaw | Could launch workloads, but policy translation, lifecycle, diagnostics, and effective-backend reporting would remain outside the existing sandbox integration. |
| Codex native Windows MXC integration | Existing upstream reference implementation | Codex provides strict `windows.sandbox = "mxc"` selection, capability probes, canonical-policy translation, and process lifetime handling. Its implementation is Windows-specific and documents networking and descendant-process limitations worth evaluating for ZeroClaw. |

### Acceptance criteria

- `mxc` is accepted and documented as an explicit sandbox backend without changing existing defaults.
- Supported Windows hosts execute commands through MXC; unsupported hosts or capabilities produce a clear error before workload launch.
- Filesystem read/write/deny rules and supported network restrictions derive from effective ZeroClaw policy, including protected paths. Unsupported policy combinations fail closed.
- Tests cover configuration, selection, capability rejection, and policy translation. Native Windows integration tests exercise real filesystem/network enforcement, stdio, exit status, timeout, cancellation, and descendant cleanup.
- Security status accurately identifies MXC and the effective containment mode, without overstating its guarantees.
- Documentation explains installation/build prerequisites, supported host capabilities, limitations, troubleshooting, and rollback.
- Existing backends continue to pass their relevant regression checks.

### Architecture impact

Affected areas include `crates/zeroclaw-config/src/schema.rs` (`SandboxBackend`), `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/` (sandbox trait, factory/detection, platform implementation and posture reporting), command execution integration, and `docs/book/src/security/sandboxing.md`.

The current sandbox abstraction should remain the entry point. Maintainers should assess whether MXC's native launch and lifecycle requirements fit the existing wrapping contract or require a narrowly scoped extension. Any live policy must continue to resolve from its canonical owner. User-facing diagnostics must follow the existing Fluent localization contract.

### Risk and rollback

The main risks are incomplete policy translation, host-dependent enforcement capabilities, lifecycle differences, Windows build/dependency costs, and accidental fallback to weaker containment. MXC's network capabilities and handling of descendant processes must be validated on actual supported hosts rather than inferred from SDK availability.

Keep MXC opt-in and leave automatic selection unchanged initially. Roll back by selecting another supported backend explicitly, or reverting the additive integration. Switching backends changes containment semantics and should be an operator decision. Diagnostics must not expose command/environment secrets.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment

### Next decision surface

Ordinary feature triage followed by a maintainer decision on Windows-first scope, SDK/build integration, and compatibility with the current sandbox execution abstraction. Maintainers can promote the design to an RFC if it changes the shared execution or policy contract.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

### References

- Microsoft MXC project and platform/backend matrix: https://github.com/microsoft/mxc
- Codex native Windows MXC integration, selection semantics and limitations (pinned source): https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/342ed69a174c206c1de52a59491b131e0753cfa5/codex-rs/mxc-sandbox/README.md
- Codex MXC policy adapter (same revision): https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/342ed69a174c206c1de52a59491b131e0753cfa5/codex-rs/mxc-sandbox/src/policy.rs

issues.body:
### Affected component

security/sandbox

### Severity

S1 - workflow blocked

### Current behavior

OIDC enrollment authenticates the client with `request.basic_auth(client_id, Some(secret))` in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/security/auth_provider/enrollment.rs`, passing the raw values. RFC 6749 §2.3.1 says the client ID and secret are form-encoded (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`) before they go into the Basic header. Introspection already does this through `form_urlencode_component`, but enrollment doesn't.

So any client ID or secret containing a reserved character fails to authenticate against a strict provider: `:`, `+`, `/`, `%` and similar. `client_credentials` and device-grant enrollment both fail. A `:` in the client ID is worse: it moves the user/password split.

### Expected behavior

Enrollment form-encodes both values before `basic_auth`, the same way introspection does, so any valid client ID and secret enroll.

A fix exists in draft #11423 (be5156721c and 86eab94be1). It applies cleanly to current master on its own, and it adds a regression that decodes the header on every enrollment endpoint and checks the round trip.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
# 1. In Keycloak, create a confidential client with service accounts enabled:
#      client ID: zc-basic: +/%
#      secret:    any value containing : + / % and the literal sequence %2B
# 2. Control, to show the provider is strict (RFC 6749 §2.3.1):
#      the form-encoded Basic pair  -> HTTP 200 and a token
#      the raw Basic pair           -> HTTP 400
# 3. Point an [oidc.<profile>] section at that client, then:
zeroclaw oidc token <profile>
# On master this fails (see the log below). With be5156721c and 86eab94be1 applied,
# it enrolls and prints a token.
```

### Impact

Affected users: anyone whose OIDC client ID or secret contains a reserved character. Generated secrets often contain `+` and `/`.
Frequency: always, for those credentials.
Consequence: enrollment fails with `unauthorized_client`. The only workaround is rotating to a secret without those characters. The behaviour has been there since enrollment was added.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
client_credentials enrollment failed: unauthorized_client (Unexpected error when authenticating client)
```

### ZeroClaw version

master 96da19523e (reproduced); the enrollment code is unchanged through master 89bd18484b

### Rust version

rustc 1.98.0

### Operating system

Linux x86_64

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Pre-flight checks

- [ ] I reproduced this on the latest master branch or latest release.
- [X] I redacted secrets, tokens, and personal data from all submitted content.

issues.body:
### TL;DR

v0.8.3 shipped with **three parallel provenance/signing mechanisms** — cosign bundles, GitHub artifact attestations, and slsa-github-generator — from two PRs that landed 26 hours apart without seeing each other. All three work (v0.8.3 is the proof), but the redundancy costs CI time, doubles our verification story in the docs, and buries 16 downloadable artifacts under 37 verification files on the release page. This issue proposes picking **one mechanism + SBOMs + a single verification archive** (~20 assets, down from 53).

### How we got here

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Jun 15 | #7675 (Hardened CI pipeline RFC, @ConYel) opened; triage asks for a split by enforcement level |
| Jun 20 | Split request re-stated → **#8058** opened by @piiiico (release-only slice) 21 minutes later |
| Jun 22 | **#8177** opened by @ConYel — his own spin-out of the same RFC's Phase 3, overlapping territory |
| Jun 29 | **#8404** merges (implements #8058): cosign sign-blob `.bundle`s, SPDX+CycloneDX SBOMs, slsa-github-generator |
| Jun 30 | **#8277** merges (implements #8177 Phase A): `actions/attest-build-provenance`, offline `.attestation.jsonl` mirror, `trusted_root.jsonl`, `ATTESTATION-BUNDLES.md` |

Both PRs were in flight simultaneously; different authors, different mergers. No one was positioned to catch the overlap. (Process suggestion at the bottom.)

### What we ship today (v0.8.3: 53 release assets)

- 16 downloadables (10 CLI archives, 5 desktop installers, install.sh)
- 15 cosign `.bundle` + 17 `.attestation.jsonl` + `trusted_root.jsonl` + `ATTESTATION-BUNDLES.md` — **two per-artifact mechanisms doing the same core job**
- `SHA256SUMS` + 2 SBOMs (different purpose — not in question, keep)
- the slsa-github-generator jobs ran green but their `.intoto.jsonl` provenance **is not among the release assets** — orphaned output, bug regardless of the outcome here

### The three mechanisms

| | cosign `sign-blob` | GitHub attestations | slsa-github-generator |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proves | identity + integrity | + build provenance | + provenance generated in isolation from the build |
| SLSA Build level | n/a | **L2** | **L3** |
| Verify via | `cosign verify-blob` (offline-capable) | `gh attestation verify` (online; offline w/ mirrored bundle) | `slsa-verifier` |
| Note | ecosystem standard (containers, admission controllers) | best DX, GitHub end-to-end trust | strongest formal guarantee |

Corrections to the record: #8277 describes its output as SLSA L3 — `attest-build-provenance` is documented by GitHub as **Build L2**. #8404's table calls the generator L2 — the generic generator is the canonical **L3** path.

### Proposal

1. **Pick one per-artifact mechanism** (decision of this issue):
   - *Option 1 — GitHub attestations*: best DX, aligns with #8177's roadmap if it stays alive; L2
   - *Option 2 — cosign + fixed slsa-generator upload*: ecosystem-standard + formal L3; aligns with #8058 as specced
2. **Ship verification material as a single `zeroclaw-vX.Y.Z-verification.tar.gz`** (bundles/attestations + trusted root + index inside; archive listed in SHA256SUMS and attested via API). No tool requires per-artifact adjacency; discoverability moves to the archive's index and the release-body footer.
3. **Either way**: fix or remove the orphaned slsa-generator upload; update `release-verification.md`, `slsa-provenance.md`, `ci-and-actions.md`; prune the loser's Actions-allowlist entries.

Result: ~20 release assets, one documented verification story, less CI time in the release path.

### Non-goals

Deciding #8177's hardware-PGP/hermetic-builds future — that stays its own RFC. This issue only needs enough of a signal (roadmap alive vs. shelved) to pick between options 1 and 2.

### Process note

When splitting an RFC, the splitter should comment on the parent linking the child issues at creation time — #8058 and #8177 both answered the same split request without cross-linking, which is how two implementations of one requirement merged in the same week.

issues.title: [Feature]: Report Signal listener health, and show it in the dashboard's channel readiness
issues.body:
### Summary

Implement `Channel::listener_health()` for the Signal channel, so `/health` reflects whether its signal-cli event stream is actually connected and delivering, and let `/api/channels` fill the `listening` readiness row from that signal for any channel that reports it, not only webhook channels.

### Problem statement

The Signal channel listens on signal-cli's SSE endpoint (`/api/v1/events`). When the connection fails or returns an error status, `listen()` logs it and retries in its own loop with backoff ([`signal.rs` L695](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/signal.rs#L695)), so it does not return. Signal does not implement `listener_health()`, so the supervisor records the channel as `ok` before `listen()` and on every health tick while it runs ([`mark_listener_health`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/orchestrator/mod.rs#L7670), the `None` case). With signal-cli down or unreachable, `/health` therefore reports `channel:signal.<alias>` as `ok`. The listener's HTTP client also sets only a connect timeout, so a request that never gets a response, or a stream that stays open but stops delivering, is also reported as `ok`, like a working idle stream.

On the dashboard, the channel card's `listening` row is computed only for webhook channels ([`channel_readiness`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/blob/89bd18484bf4a262e43223d011306a8add031e29/crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs#L1562)). An enabled, bound Signal channel shows `listening` as "not checked" (API value `unknown`) with the note "Live readiness is not checked for `signal` channels yet." That is the honest answer #6985 chose, but it stays that way even for channels that do report listener health, such as Telegram (#10005) and WASM plugin channels (#11348).

### Proposed solution

Building on #6985 and #8732 (channel-owned readiness) and #10005 (passive listener health, no active probing on a timer):

1. **Signal implements `listener_health()`** from what its listener already observes, recording the time of each successful connect and of every received chunk, and starting again from `Pending` whenever `listen()` is entered:
   - `Pending` until the first connect attempt completes, but `Unhealthy` if an attempt is still waiting for a response after the staleness limit;
   - `Healthy` while the last successful connect or chunk is within the staleness limit and no connect attempt has failed since;
   - `Unhealthy` after a failed connect or error status, or when nothing has arrived for longer than the limit.

   signal-cli writes a `:` keepalive comment on the event stream every 15 seconds (configurable with `--sse-keepalive-interval` since v0.14.9), so chunks arrive even when there are no messages. Time the listener spends processing an event before reading the next chunk should not count as silence (or the limit must cover it). The limit should be generous, for example about three keepalive intervals, which also lets a routine reconnect (the listener waits 2s before retrying) finish without reporting `Unhealthy`; an operator who raises the keepalive interval above the limit would see the channel as unhealthy, so the limit should be documented or configurable. This reports the ZeroClaw-to-signal-cli event stream, not signal-cli's own connection to the Signal service.
2. **`/api/channels` fills `listening` from the health registry** for channels that report listener health. For those channels, a fresh `ok` maps to `ready`; a fresh `starting` maps to `unknown` with a note that the listener is starting; `error`, anything stale or no entry maps to `missing`, as webhook does today. The existing "Live readiness is not checked…" note is replaced for those channels (only authentication then remains unchecked). Webhook, which also maps `starting` to `missing`, keeps its current mapping. Two details for the implementation:
   - The registry records `ok` both for a reported `Healthy` and for the `None` fallback, so readiness needs to tell the two apart, for example with an additive field on the component's health entry saying whether the status came from the channel's own signal (it would appear in the health snapshot served by `/api/status`, `/api/health`, RPC and the daemon state file, and in the generated OpenAPI schema; the public `/health` lists its fields explicitly), or with a channel-owned capability lookup like `zeroclaw_channels::listing::qr_pairing_channel`. Errors the supervisor records when `listen()` exits would count as `missing` for a reporting channel.
   - The readiness freshness limit (`CHANNEL_LISTENER_HEALTH_MAX_AGE_SECS`, 30s) equals the supervisor's heartbeat (30s), so a healthy listener can briefly read stale; it should allow a margin, for example twice the heartbeat. The same edge exists today for webhook channels, which share the constant and would get the same margin.

   Channels that report nothing stay `unknown` with the existing note.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Active probing (`health_check()`) on a timer or per dashboard request.
- Recovering a listener that reports `Unhealthy` (tracked for Telegram in #11608, which proposes restarting it and/or adding request timeouts). For Signal, an idle timeout inside `listen()` that drops a silent stream and reconnects would be a small follow-up.
- `listener_health()` for other channels; email and others could follow the same pattern separately.
- The `authenticated` readiness row. With it still `unknown`, a Signal card summarizes as `unknown`/`degraded` when listening is `ready` and `error`/`down` when it is `missing`.

### Alternatives considered

- Calling Signal's existing `health_check()` (`GET /api/v1/check`) from the readiness request: simple, but it is an active call per request, #10005 kept active probes out of recurring health paths, and it only shows that signal-cli's HTTP server is up, not that the listener's event stream is connected.
- Leaving Signal on the default: keeps `/health` reporting `ok` for a Signal channel that cannot reach signal-cli.

### Acceptance criteria

- With signal-cli unreachable, `/health` reports the Signal channel as `error` at the next supervisor health tick after a connect attempt has failed or has waited longer than the staleness limit (`starting` before that), and returns to `ok` at the next tick after the stream connects.
- A stream that stays open but receives nothing, keepalives included, for longer than the limit is reported `Unhealthy`.
- For a channel that reports listener health, `/api/channels` shows `listening: ready` when its entry is `ok` and fresh, `unknown` while it is `starting`, and `missing` when it is `error`, stale or absent; channels without a listener-health signal stay `unknown`.
- Unit tests for the Signal state transitions and staleness, and an API-boundary test for the readiness row, as #8732 did.

### Architecture impact

- `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/signal.rs`: recorded times and `listener_health()`.
- Either the health registry in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/health` and `mark_listener_health` (an added field on the component's health entry, which the generated OpenAPI schema in `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/openapi.rs` then includes), or `crates/zeroclaw-channels/src/listing.rs` (a capability lookup).
- `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api.rs`: `channel_readiness` and the readiness freshness limit.

No config change unless the staleness limit is made configurable; `listener_health()` already exists on the trait with a default.

### Risk and rollback

Low to medium. It changes what `/health` and the channel card report for Signal, and the readiness logic shared by all channels: Telegram and plugin channel cards would have their `listening` row filled in and could now summarize as `error`/`down` when their listener reports unhealthy. Rollback is reverting the PR(s). #11556 (open) also touches `signal.rs`, including `listen()`, so whichever lands second needs a rebase.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Whether the readiness change should be in the same PR as Signal's `listener_health()` or a separate one, and how readiness should tell a channel-reported status from the default. I can open a PR once the shape is agreed.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.title: [Feature]: Long-running shell tasks with async/sync modes and a user-operated interactive terminal
issues.body:
### Summary

Support long-running shell tasks with explicit asynchronous and synchronous execution modes, plus a separate interactive terminal where users can enter input directly.

### Problem statement

The built-in shell call currently waits for completion within a configured timeout, closes stdin, and does not expose an interactive terminal. This makes two common workflows difficult:

- Builds, training scripts, and development servers can exceed the shell timeout. The agent needs to wait briefly for fast completion, then continue its turn while a longer task keeps running.
- Commands that request passwords, confirmations, or other terminal input need a user-operated terminal. Increasing a timeout does not provide that input path.

Related issue #1404 proposed background process management but explicitly excluded writing to stdin. This request covers explicit wait/timeout semantics and a user-facing interactive terminal; the historical background-process implementation should be assessed for reuse during design.

### Proposed solution

#### 1. Long-running script tasks

Expose an execution mode and mode-specific parameters in the model-facing tool schema. The parameter names below are illustrative; the behavior is the requirement.

**Asynchronous mode (`mode: "async"`, `wait_secs`)**

- Let the model pass the initial waiting duration with each call.
- Keep the tool call and the current turn blocked while the command runs within that waiting window.
- If the command finishes during the window, return its output and exit status immediately.
- If the window expires first, keep the same process running in the background, return a stable task handle, and let the turn continue. Do not restart the command during this transition.
- Background execution has no elapsed-time execution limit: the initial waiting duration is not a timeout. A task continues until it exits, is explicitly stopped, or its execution owner shuts down. This does not require surviving a daemon restart.
- Provide operations to inspect task status, retrieve incremental output and final exit status, and explicitly stop the task and its process group.

**Synchronous mode (`mode: "sync"`, `timeout_secs`)**

- Allow the execution timeout to be set per call.
- Keep the tool call and the current turn blocked until the command completes, reaches that timeout, or is cancelled.
- Return output and exit status on completion. On timeout, terminate the process group and return a clear timeout result; do not silently move the task into the background.

Validate mode-specific parameters and document their units, defaults, and cancellation behavior. In asynchronous mode, outer turn deadlines must not silently become background task execution deadlines after the task has been handed off.

#### 2. User-operated interactive shell

- Allow opening a separate terminal window or terminal pane backed by a PTY, where the user can directly interact with the shell or launched command.
- Support manual input for password prompts, confirmations, and similar interactive flows. Input must go directly to the terminal process; passwords must not be routed through the model, conversation history, tool receipts, or application logs. Preserve terminal echo behavior so password entry stays hidden when the command disables echo.
- Support live terminal output, normal terminal input, resize events, and interruption.
- Give the user a clear way to end the interactive session. On session end, window/pane closure, explicit cancellation, or owner shutdown, terminate and reap the owned process group so descendants are not left running. Use the platform-equivalent process-tree cleanup mechanism where Unix process groups are unavailable.
- If the current client cannot provide an interactive terminal, report that limitation clearly rather than launching an inaccessible prompt.

### Non-goals / out of scope

- Having the model collect, store, or type the user's passwords.
- Bypassing command approvals, sandboxing, tool visibility, or ownership checks.
- Persisting running processes across daemon restarts.
- A general-purpose remote desktop or terminal multiplexer.

### Alternatives considered

- Increase the existing shell timeout: helps some batch jobs but blocks the turn for the whole run and does not provide manual input.
- Run commands manually outside ZeroClaw and paste results back: loses task status and lifecycle integration.
- Use detached shell commands or external terminal multiplexers: leaves process ownership, cleanup, and result retrieval to the user.
- Add only a stdin-write operation: may help automation, but does not provide the requested separate user-operated terminal or full terminal semantics.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The model-facing schema exposes asynchronous and synchronous execution modes with validated wait/timeout parameters.
- [ ] An asynchronous command finishing within `wait_secs` returns its result without waiting for the entire window.
- [ ] An asynchronous command exceeding `wait_secs` returns a task handle, releases the turn, and continues as the same process without an execution timeout.
- [ ] Background tasks expose status, incremental output, final exit status, and explicit process-group cancellation.
- [ ] A synchronous command blocks the turn until completion, cancellation, or its per-call timeout; timeout terminates the process group and reports the timeout.
- [ ] A supported client opens a separate interactive terminal window/pane and allows the user to answer prompts directly, including passwords with terminal echo disabled.
- [ ] Ending or closing an interactive session terminates and reaps its owned process group, including descendants.
- [ ] Password input is absent from model context, conversation history, tool receipts, and application logs.
- [ ] Existing approval, sandbox, and task ownership boundaries remain enforced for task creation and subsequent control operations.
- [ ] Tests cover the wait-to-background transition without duplicate execution, synchronous timeout, task cancellation, terminal input/echo handling, and descendant cleanup. User-facing documentation explains both modes and interactive-session lifecycle.

### Architecture impact

Shell tool schema and execution, runtime task ownership/cancellation, background task status/output, terminal/PTY management, client UI, security boundaries, and documentation.

The runtime should identify the canonical owner and task record for each running process and reuse existing lifecycle facilities where appropriate, rather than adding competing process registries. Maintainers should assess how an interactive terminal integrates with the supported clients and whether the design crosses an RFC trigger.

### Risk and rollback

Unlimited-duration background tasks can consume resources until explicitly stopped. Interactive sessions can expose sensitive terminal content or leave descendants behind if ownership and cleanup are incomplete. Keep these modes explicit, preserve existing authorization and isolation, bound retained output independently of execution duration, and provide visible stop controls and deterministic cleanup. Disabling the new modes restores the existing shell execution behavior; stop and clean up owned tasks/sessions when disabling them.

### Expected routing

Needs maintainer design assessment

### Next decision surface

Maintainer assessment of the shell task lifecycle and supported-client interactive terminal UX, including reuse of the historical work linked from #1404. Confirm implementation scope and promote to an RFC only if required by the repository's architecture rules.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [x] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [x] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
### Task

Apply the pinned-dial address cap once per WebSocket dial, not once per retry round, so one `dial_authorized` call reaches at most `MAX_DIAL_ADDRESSES` (8) distinct addresses.

### Context

#11814 (for #11813) adds a shared staggered dialer, `connect_pinned_addresses` in `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/egress.rs`. Each call interleaves the address families and keeps the first eight addresses.

The WebSocket dialer, `dial_authorized` in `crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/component_websocket.rs`, calls it once per round. When an address connects and then fails TLS or the WebSocket handshake, the dialer drops that address from `remaining` and calls the dialer again on the rest. Each call applies the cap afresh, so a ninth address moves into the window. With nine or more pinned addresses whose handshakes fail fast, one WebSocket dial can connect to more than eight distinct addresses.

The 10 s connect deadline, the outer 30 s WebSocket bound, the four-in-flight limit and the address pinning all still hold, so this is not a liveness or authorization problem. The cap just isn't the per-dial guarantee its doc comment describes. `wasi:http` (`dial_pinned`) and raw sockets (`connect_pinned`) dial once per connection and already stay within it.

This came up in the review of #11814 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11814#discussion_r4302223795) and in both approvals, which accepted it as a non-blocking follow-up.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One `dial_authorized` call dials at most `MAX_DIAL_ADDRESSES` distinct addresses across all its rounds. They are chosen by the same family interleaving as a single `connect_pinned_addresses` call.
- [ ] The interleave-and-cap step lives in one `egress.rs` helper that both `connect_pinned_addresses` and the WebSocket retry loop use.
- [ ] A test with more than eight pinned addresses whose TLS or WebSocket handshakes fail fast asserts that exactly eight are reached. It fails with the per-round cap.
- [ ] Unchanged: the connect deadline, the in-flight limit, the 250 ms stagger, the pinning, and which error is reported. An address refused in an earlier round may still be dialed again in a later one, as #11814 documents.

### Likely files or areas

- crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/egress.rs
- crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/component_websocket.rs

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

JordanTheJet. The fix and its test are ready and open as a PR once #11814 merges.

### Risk notes

This touches every WebSocket plugin connection, but it can only reduce the number of addresses one dial reaches. It builds on #11814's dialer, so it waits for #11814 to merge.

issues.body:
### Task

Make the repair command printed by a lifecycle-directory refusal treat a path that starts with `-` as a path, so pasting the command fixes startup.

### Context

#11803 moves the config lifecycle lock into `data/.lifecycle`. When that directory fails its checks, ZeroClaw refuses to start and prints a command that fixes it: `rm <path>` for a link or other non-directory, `chmod 700 <path>` for a group- or world-writable directory, or `sudo chown -R <user> <path>` for one another account owns.

`remedy_command` in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/live_config_authority.rs` shell-quotes the path but otherwise prints it as given. A relative config directory is used as given (only `~` is expanded), so `ZEROCLAW_CONFIG_DIR=-install` can produce `rm -install/data/.lifecycle` or `chmod 700 -install/data/.lifecycle`. `rm` on Linux and macOS, and GNU `chmod`, read that path as options and fail (`chmod: invalid option -- 'i'`), so the printed fix does nothing.

Adding `--`, as suggested in the review, doesn't work on macOS. BSD `chmod` and `chown` stop reading options at the mode or owner, so `chmod 700 -- <path>` and `chown -R <user> -- <path>` fail with `--: No such file or directory`. A `./` prefix works for all three commands on both systems.

This came up in the review of #11803 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11803#discussion_r4299809249) and in both approvals, which accepted it as non-blocking.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A relative path whose first component starts with `-` is printed so that `rm`, `chmod` and `chown` read it as a path on Linux and macOS, for example `./-install/data/.lifecycle`. Every other path prints exactly as before.
- [ ] A test runs the printed `chmod 700` and `rm` commands through `sh -c` from the directory the path is relative to, checks that they worked, and fails without the fix.
- [ ] The refusal text, its Fluent messages and the checks that trigger it are unchanged.

### Likely files or areas

- crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/live_config_authority.rs (`remedy_command` and its tests)

### Contributor fit

maintainer-scoped task, not yet ready for pickup labels

### Mentor, reviewer, or contact

JordanTheJet. The fix and its test are ready and open as a PR once #11803 merges.

### Risk notes

Only the printed command text changes, and only for a relative data directory whose first component starts with `-`. PR CI runs the new test on Linux. BSD `chmod` and `chown` on macOS are covered by the scheduled platform run and were checked by hand.

issues.body:
### Affected component

plugins

### Severity

S3 - minor issue

### Current behavior

With `plugins.security.signature_mode = "strict"`, plugin discovery skips every unsigned package. The CLI then reports those packages as if they were not on disk:

```text
$ zeroclaw plugin info discord
Error: Plugin 'discord' not found.
$ zeroclaw plugin list --verify
No plugins installed.
```

Both packages (`discord` and `redact-text`, installed from the registry, which publishes them unsigned) are present in the plugins directory. Only the daemon log says why they are ignored:

```text
WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", "plugin": "<config-dir>/plugins/discord"}
```

Where it happens:

- Discovery checks the signature and, on failure, records the warning and drops the package (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/host.rs:349`, record at `:394`).
- `PluginHost::get_plugin` and `list_plugins` read only the admitted set (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/host.rs:446`, `:454`).
- `plugin info` turns `None` into `cli-plugin-not-found` (`src/main.rs:12718`), and `plugin list --verify` prints `cli-plugins-none` for an empty set (`src/main.rs:3644`).

`plugin remove` already handles this case: for a package the host did not load it reports admission's own verdict, such as the unsigned refusal (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/host.rs:2610`, test `remove_refuses_a_valid_package_it_did_not_load` at `:5165`). `info` and `list` do not.

A related point: one daemon start under `strict` wrote the discord skip warning 6 times (and the redact-text one 5 times) within 140 ms. Each subsystem builds its own `PluginHost`, and each construction runs discovery and logs again: the channel plugins (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/plugin_runtime.rs:1077`), the tool registry (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/tools/mod.rs:2527`, which its own comment says also runs per gateway request), plugin skills (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/skills/mod.rs:3267`), and the gateway's plugin API (`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/api_plugins.rs:203`).

### Expected behavior

- `plugin info <name>` for a package that is on disk but refused by the trust policy names the refusal and the setting behind it (for example: installed, not loaded because `signature_mode = strict` and the package is unsigned), and exits non-zero.
- `plugin list --verify` lists such packages with a "not loaded: <reason>" verdict instead of reporting nothing installed.
- A daemon start logs each skip once, or at least once per subsystem in a way that reads as one decision.

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
zeroclaw plugin install discord            # registry packages are unsigned
zeroclaw plugin info discord               # Loads: yes
zeroclaw config set --no-interactive plugins.security.signature_mode strict
zeroclaw plugin info discord               # Error: Plugin 'discord' not found.
zeroclaw plugin list --verify              # No plugins installed.
zeroclaw daemon                            # skip warning repeated per subsystem
```

### Impact

Anyone who turns on `strict` with registry packages installed. Every registry package is unsigned today, so `strict` turns all of them off, and the CLI's answer ("not found", "No plugins installed") points the operator at reinstalling instead of at the trust setting.

### Logs / stack traces

```text
09:32:23.620Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.653Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.746Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.753Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.753Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.760Z WARN skipping plugin due to signature verification failure {"error": "plugin 'discord' is unsigned and signature verification is required", ...}
09:32:23.760Z INFO Registered WASM channel plugins {"admitted": 0, "constructed": 0}
```

### ZeroClaw version

v0.8.6 release-candidate build (61a2c95); code references are to current master

### Operating system

Ubuntu 24.04 (WSL2)

### Regression?

No, first-time setup

### Related

#11811 (reports the runtime's config refusal in the same two commands, for loaded tools only), #10999

issues.body:
### Task

Record where a claimed package came from in its recovery transaction, so an interrupted `plugin remove` puts it back where it was.

### Context

With #11809, `plugin remove` of a loaded plugin claims the directory the plugin was loaded from, which may be named differently from the manifest. If the remove stops between the claim and the deletion mark, or the put-back after a failed identity check fails, the next remove settles the unmarked claim the way recovery settles any other: it publishes it to `<plugins_dir>/<name>` with no-replace. So the package comes back at `<name>`, not at the directory it came from, and while something unrelated occupies `<name>` every later remove refuses until that is moved aside by hand. Nothing is deleted or overwritten; #11809 documents the behaviour and the manual way out.

### Acceptance criteria

issues.body:
### Summary

Give the standalone gateway a service identity of its own for its daemon connection, scoped to `channels:execute` on the channel instances it forwards.

### Problem statement

With #11322 and the default `security.trust_daemon_uid = true`, the standalone `zeroclaw gateway` connects to the daemon socket as the shared operator, which holds every grant. Its forwarder needs only `channels:execute`, which #11320 scopes to named channel instances with `allowed_channels`.

This is not an escalation: anything running as that uid could dial the socket itself. The connection is also kept out of the `CoreRpc` extension, so no other route can reach it. Still, the gateway holds far more authority than it uses, and the daemon's audit records cannot tell the gateway apart from an operator.

The in-process seam from #11186 stays idle for the same reason. The gateway has no credential of its own to present: `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/core_rpc.rs` lists a service key or a forwarded user bearer as later work. Neither #11002 (standalone zeroclaw-gw) nor #11001 (local IPC coverage) tracks this. The maintainer review of #11322 asked for an issue so the deferral is tracked rather than implied.

### Proposed solution

A gateway service principal that the forwarder presents in its `initialize`:

- for example a dedicated service credential, or a roster entry for the gateway's uid with `security.trust_daemon_uid = false`;
- mapped to a permission profile with `channels = ["execute"]` and `allowed_channels` naming the instances it serves;
- audited as the gateway.

Document the deployment next to the existing `ZEROCLAW_SOCKET` setup in `docs/book/src/gateway/api.md`.

### Non-goals / out of scope

Forwarded end-user bearer identity, WSS or remote gateways, and Windows forwarding.

### Alternatives considered

Keep the shared operator (today's behavior, documented): workable, but the gateway's authority is broader than its job and its actions are indistinguishable in audit.

### Acceptance criteria

- The standalone gateway can connect with a configured scoped principal, and the daemon audits its actions under it.
- With that principal, a dispatch to an unlisted channel instance is refused.
- The docs describe the setup, and the two-process e2e covers it.

### Architecture impact

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/core_rpc.rs` and the forwarder, runtime principal resolution (`crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/auth.rs`), config (gateway or users section), and the gateway API and authentication docs.

### Risk and rollback

A misconfigured principal leaves the gateway unable to forward (503 on `/plugin/{path}`). Rollback: the shared-operator default stays available.

### Expected routing

Should attach to an existing roadmap/tracker issue

### Next decision surface

#11002 (standalone zeroclaw-gw) under #7432's gateway split, where the gateway's credential model is decided.

### Breaking change?

No

### Data hygiene checks

- [X] I removed personal/sensitive data from examples, payloads, and logs.
- [X] I used neutral, project-focused wording and placeholders.

issues.body:
### Summary

Leave one standalone gateway path, so `run_gateway` does not serve a silently unrouted `/plugin/{path}`.

### Problem statement

After #11322, `zeroclaw gateway` forwards `/plugin/{path}` to the daemon, but `zeroclaw_gateway::run_gateway` and `run_gateway_with_authority` still serve a route that answers 404 for every path:

- `src/main.rs` no longer calls them; they are reached only from `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/acp.rs`, the gateway's lib tests and `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/tests/golden_frames.rs`.
- `zeroclaw-gateway` is a published crate, so an embedder on Unix gets the old dead route with no log line.
- The `run_gateway_with_authority` doc comment ("with the live config authority owned by its daemon generation") is stale for these standalone callers.

The maintainer review of #11322 suggested one standalone path.

### Proposed solution

Either:

- route `run_gateway` through `GatewaySupervision::standalone`, so embedders forward plugin webhooks the way `zeroclaw gateway` does; or
- narrow it to test support, leaving `run_gateway_with_plugin_webhooks` with an explicit `GatewaySupervision` as the embedding entry point.

At minimum, log once at startup when a gateway runs with no route source, and fix the stale doc comment.

### Non-goals / out of scope

No change to the supervised gateway, the forwarder, or the forwarding deployment.

### Alternatives considered

Keep both paths and document the difference: the behavior gap stays silent for embedders.

### Acceptance criteria

- One documented standalone entry point.
- An embedder either forwards plugin webhooks or gets an explicit startup log saying they are unrouted.
- Tests and the doc comment are updated.

### Architecture impact

`crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/lib.rs` (entry points), `crates/zeroclaw-gateway/src/acp.rs`, and the gateway tests.

### Risk and rollback

Routing through `standalone` changes embedders' `/plugin/{path}` from 404 to forwarding; narrowing changes the public API of an experimental crate. Rollback: revert.

### Expected routing

Ordinary feature triage

### Next decision surface

Ordinary triage. Lands after #11322.

### Breaking change?

No

issues.body:
### Summary

State the `plugin-webhook/dispatch` wire bounds in the generated OpenRPC schema.

### Problem statement

`PluginWebhookDispatchParams.method` is a `String` documented as `GET` or `POST`. The other bounds live only in doc comments and `docs/book/src/architecture/rpc-socket.md`:

- `request_id`: 1 to 128 bytes of printable ASCII;
- `headers`: at most 512 entries and 524,288 bytes;
- `query`: at most 65,536 bytes;
- `body_b64`: at most 65,536 decoded bytes.

The generated document (`docs/book/src/architecture/zeroclaw-rpc.openrpc.json`) does not state them, so a client learns them only from `INVALID_PARAMS` at runtime. The maintainer review of #11320 suggested putting them in the schema.

### Proposed solution

- A two-variant enum for `method` (serialized as `GET` and `POST`).
- `schemars` length, pattern and item-count attributes on the other fields, taken from the shared `MAX_PLUGIN_WEBHOOK_*` constants in `zeroclaw_api::webhook` so the schema cannot drift from enforcement.

The shared `PluginWebhookRequest::new` validation stays the authority.

### Non-goals / out of scope

No change to the bounds, to validation, or to the wire format.

### Alternatives considered

Leave the bounds in prose: clients cannot check them mechanically.

### Acceptance criteria

- The OpenRPC document states each bound, and a test ties the schema values to the `MAX_PLUGIN_WEBHOOK_*` constants.
- Serde round-trip tests show the wire format is unchanged.
- `cargo run -p xtask --bin generate -- openrpc --check` passes.

### Architecture impact

`zeroclaw-rpc-proto` (types and schema catalog) and the regenerated OpenRPC document.

### Risk and rollback

Low; wire-compatible as long as serde names stay the same. Rollback: revert.

### Expected routing

Could become contributor-ready after maintainer scoping

### Next decision surface

Ordinary triage. Lands after #11320, which defines these types.

### Breaking change?

No

prs.title: fix(rpc): judge queued session ownership by current authority
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`. Current head: `d72bab13cd71f1fa31e0028668a2ee471a88f9fc`, integrating master through `ceb1e11176b7ee86ca3007cb7f6110ae94ff6ecb`. This adopts the [prepared canonical repair](https://github.com/Aarlington/zeroclaw/commit/677961e7d73f17c36a7d21742095ea0292d605d8) by fast-forward, preserves the original PR history, and retains the merged #10246 and #11222 behavior.
- **What changed and why:**
  - Session operations that wait (for the session admission permit, the config writer gate, a pending provider binding or the provider-update lock) decided ownership with the administrator bypass stamped on the connection before the wait. `recheck_authority_after_admission` re-resolved the grants afterwards but never updated that stamp, so an administrator demoted while queued still reached another principal's session. A new `scoped_principal_id_from(grants)` derives the ownership scope from a given grant set; `scoped_principal_id()` delegates to it with the stamped grants and remains the pre-wait check. `revalidate_admitted_session`, `authorize_session_owner_for_mode` and `resolve_session_record_for_mode` now take the scope as a parameter instead of reading the stamp, so those post-admission ownership decisions and refusals use freshly resolved grants.
  - `session/close`, `session/kill` and `session/delete` recheck authority right after the permit and revalidate with the scope those grants give. Kill and delete also fall back to the durable record when a hard-cancelled turn removed the live incarnation during the wait; that fallback now requires the record to be the caller's under the same scope. Without it, a demoted administrator whose target's live incarnation disappeared while it waited still tombstoned or deleted another principal's durable row.
  - `session/prompt` derives ownership from fresh grants after admission and provider waits. Final preparation runs inside the execution task after it acquires the canonical Agent lock. It checks the exact Agent and current owner/binding/environment permissions, narrows tools, and authorizes the checkpoint or running-state write under the storage lock before execution. Refused preparation ends the client turn through `refuse_admitted_prompt` without calling the provider. Rehydration uses guarded recovery and seed-trim persistence so a storage-lock wait cannot retain earlier authority.
  - `session/new`: `SessionStore::resume_existing_authorized` hands the session's owner to its authorize closure, and the new `authorize_resumed_incarnation` judges that owner with the same authority it resolves for the agent/workspace binding and the retained environment, under the store lock. A connection whose stamp still carries a revoked bypass therefore cannot rebind another principal's live session. After the permit, authority is re-resolved before anything else and the scope derived from it judges the record found under the permit (so a demoted administrator no longer leaves a cross-principal audit record for a request refused a few lines later, and a principal promoted while waiting is honoured), the post-admission resume, the cross-mode replacement and the ACP restore preload. After the config writer gate wait it is re-derived again: the owner of the session being restored or replaced must match, and whether a failed owner-stamp write aborts creation follows that scope.
  - `session/configure` and the queued (reaped) branch of `session/messages` also act after a wait and call `revalidate_admitted_session`, so they recheck authority and pass the fresh scope as well.
  - Live cancellation, publication and deferred approval-channel installation reauthorize under the live-session boundary. `session/messages` and plan replay reserve outbound capacity before their final ownership/authority check and send synchronously while guarded. The shared plan helper covers live resume, restored `session/new`, and prompt rehydration.
  - `session/append` passes the current ownership scope into its admitted lookup, then resolves authority again after that awaited lookup and before either transcript write. Its regression covers a demoted administrator targeting a foreign session, an owner whose update grant was revoked, and a demoted owner whose update grant remains valid.
- **Scope boundary:** The request gate, durable owner identity (`owner_principal_id`), wire, config and CLI shapes are unchanged. Ownership after the covered waits follows current authority. The guards authorize individual effects; this does not add continuous revocation of an already-admitted running turn or roll back effects authorized before demotion.
- **Blast radius:** RPC dispatch, execution-task preparation, live-session synchronization, outbound frame reservation, and guarded ACP/Chat persistence. New authorization callbacks run after storage locks or transactions are acquired and retain authority through synchronous effects. History helpers acquire the Agent before the session map and recheck incarnation identity. Unsupported guarded backend reads and deletes fail closed. Permitted own-session operations retain positive-control coverage.
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11126. Related #11222 (merged prerequisite). Related #10412.

### What this does, simply

Named local principals can hold an administrator bypass that lets them act on other principals' sessions. Several session requests wait before they act: behind a turn that holds the session, behind a configuration change, or behind a provider update. The daemon did recheck the caller's permissions after that wait, but it kept deciding who owns what from the administrator flag recorded when the request arrived. If an administrator lost that role while their request waited, the request still went through: it could delete another person's saved session, kill it, send it a prompt, change its settings, read it, or restore it.

After this change, the covered effects decide ownership from the permissions in force after their final wait. A demoted administrator receives the same "not found or not owned" refusal as any other principal before that effect executes, changes saved data, or discloses a foreign transcript or plan. Permitted operations on the caller's own sessions keep working.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: reproducing it needs a principal roster and a demotion that lands while a request is queued, which the dispatcher-level regressions below drive deterministically.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** No current-head CI result is claimed yet; [Quality Gate for `d72bab13cd71f1fa31e0028668a2ee471a88f9fc`](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38948140056) is running. The local checks below cover the changed RPC, storage, live-authority and API crates on macOS arm64; the broader workspace, feature matrix and parallel runtime checks remain pending.
- **Current-head local validation:** `d72bab13cd71f1fa31e0028668a2ee471a88f9fc` (tree `0cb5396b9b114b24801ab91e4a87f00e433c7974`), macOS arm64, rustc 1.97.1; default crate features and eight test threads. All 1,094 focused tests passed, with no Clippy diagnostics.

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check
# exit 0; no output
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib rpc:: -- --test-threads=8
# 862 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 4919 filtered out
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-infra --lib session -- --test-threads=8
# 207 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 107 filtered out
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib live_config_authority:: -- --test-threads=8
# 25 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 5756 filtered out
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-api -p zeroclaw-infra -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
# Finished dev profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 2m 19s
```

- **Linker diagnostic:** The macOS runtime test link emitted `ld: __eh_frame section too large (max 16MB)`; the binary linked and every selected test ran successfully. A clean checkout of pinned master `ceb1e11176b7ee86ca3007cb7f6110ae94ff6ecb` reproduces the identical diagnostic with `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib --no-run` (exit 0); it comes from the large debug test binary's unwind section and is not introduced by this PR.

- **Historical CI on the previous PR head (not current-head evidence):** On `d5df4214cad96bfc6bfbdea13a64767b116ac1df`, [Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36751197781/job/110009962176), [Parallel Runtime Test](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36751197781/job/110010144453), Lint, the plugin-backend Check legs, and the [CI Required Gate](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/36751197781/job/110014127332) pass. The Test log explicitly records the admission/provider, final-effect, storage-lock and outbound-backpressure regressions below passing; its main suite reports 19,059 passed and 39 skipped. These results cover only that older revision; the refreshed head has a separate run.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Current local evidence exercises synthetic principals, in-process RPC handlers, existing local/WSS transport tests and real session stores on macOS; it does not prove a live daemon against a real identity provider. Linux, Windows and feature-matrix coverage for the refreshed head awaits the linked CI run; older CI and local results below are historical evidence only.
- **Regression coverage:**
  - `append_rechecks_authority_after_admitted_lookup` (prepared-repair regression): demotion cannot preserve a foreign-session append, and revoking an owner's update grant prevents both durable and live writes; a demoted owner who retains update authority can still append.
  - `queued_operations_lose_the_admin_bypass_when_the_administrator_is_demoted` (new): alice holds `member` session grants plus an `administrator` profile, and bob owns an ACP session. For each of prompt, close, delete and kill against bob's live session, delete and kill when its live incarnation is reaped during the wait, and prompt (the rehydration path) and messages against the reaped session, alice's request passes its pre-check as administrator and parks on the admission permit; the profile loses `admin` (her `member` grants stay) and the permit is released. Each request gets `FORBIDDEN` with the uniform denial, each refused prompt ends the client's turn with a failed `TurnComplete` on alice's connection, bob's live generation is unchanged (or the session stays reaped, not revived), and his durable row still exists, is not killed, keeps his owner and gains no messages. Configure parked on the provider-update lock is refused the same way and bob's overrides are unchanged. Positive control: alice, demoted while her delete of her own session waits, deletes it.
  - `queued_prompt_rechecks_ownership_after_its_provider_waits` (new): alice's prompt on bob's live session passes the post-admission ownership check as administrator and then parks, once on the provider-update lock and once on a pending provider binding; she is demoted and the wait is released. Both prompts get `FORBIDDEN` with the uniform denial and a failed `TurnComplete`, bob's provider receives no call, and his incarnation and durable row are unchanged.
  - `demoted_administrator_cannot_resume_a_foreign_session_with_a_stale_stamp` (new): `handle_session_new_for_test` skips the gate, so alice's connection keeps its administrator stamp after the demotion; `session/new` naming bob's live session is refused and his generation is unchanged, while the same stale connection still rebinds a session of her own. Resumes of bob's reaped ACP and chat sessions queued behind the permit when the demotion lands are refused and nothing is restored; bob's ACP row keeps an interrupted-turn checkpoint unrecovered and his chat row keeps its owner. Positive control: her own reaped ACP session, resumed the same way, is restored.
  - The direct `resume_existing_authorized` tests accept the owner argument and returned authorization guard.
  - `final_prompt_effect_waits_recheck_current_authority`, `removal_effect_waits_preserve_foreign_session_after_demotion`, `restore_effect_waits_preserve_retained_checkpoint_after_demotion`, and `deferred_approval_install_rechecks_after_agent_wait` cover the later execution, mutation and channel-install boundaries.

The plan-backpressure matrix now includes remote live and cross-mode resume and checks their intended admission-permit lifetimes.
- **Commands run and tail output** (author-reported historical local evidence on b0879527d3, macOS arm64, rustc 1.98.0; not a claim of new local runs on the integrated head):
  - `cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-runtime -E 'test(/admitted|demot|owner|resume|queued/)'`: `114 tests run: 114 passed, 5169 skipped`.
  - `TMPDIR=/private/tmp cargo nextest run -p zeroclaw-runtime -E 'test(/rpc::/)'`: `660 tests run: 660 passed, 4623 skipped`.
  - `./scripts/ci/rust_quality_gate.sh --strict`: fmt passes; clippy stops on its only error, `unused import: std::sync::mpsc` at `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/src/service/mod.rs:15`, which unmodified `master` also reports on macOS (the import is used only by Windows and Linux code). The script's provider-dispatch section, run on its own: `provider dispatch gate clean`.
  - `cargo clippy --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets --features ci-all -- -D warnings -A unused_imports`: `Finished`, no diagnostics.
  - `cargo doc --no-deps --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop`: `Finished`, no warnings.
  - `./scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh`: `Comment hygiene gate passed.`
  - `cargo test --no-run --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop`: every test target builds; its only warnings are the two macOS-only ones unmodified `master` emits (the `std::sync::mpsc` import and the `ld: __eh_frame section too large` linker note), so allowing `unused_imports` above hides nothing new.
  - `TMPDIR=/private/tmp ZEROCLAW_PARALLEL_TEST_RUNS=1 ./scripts/ci/parallel_runtime_test_gate.sh`: `zeroclaw-runtime` `5231 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored`, `zeroclaw-channels` `1957 passed; 0 failed; 2 ignored`.
  - Plugin-backend commands from `check-plugin-backends`, run as written (the change filter reports `true` for this diff). The two `zeroclaw-runtime` legs ran on this commit; the rest ran on the previous revision of it, which differs only in `rpc/dispatch.rs`:
    - `cargo check --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --no-default-features --features` `plugins-wasm-cranelift` / `plugins-wasm-pulley` / `plugins-wasmtime`: all `Finished`.
    - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test channel_plugin_e2e --test egress_plugin_e2e --test tool_plugin_timeout_e2e --test reference_plugin --test reference_plugin_e2e --test tool_plugin_e2e`: every binary `ok`, 43 passed, 0 failed.
    - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --no-default-features --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib`: `260 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib agent::plugin_live_config`: `2 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib -- plugin_runtime:: tools::tests::shared_ceiling tools::tests::repeated_loader tools::tests::auto_discover tools::tests::colliding_plugin`: `22 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test plugin_channel_runtime_e2e`: `4 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test channel_egress_e2e`: `3 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --bin zeroclaw`: `551 passed; 0 failed`.
    - `cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test component -- plugin_info_cli`: `4 passed; 0 failed`.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Historical author verification on b0879527d3 and the earlier revisions noted below (not newly repeated on the integrated head): confirmed the regressions fail without the fix by mutating one path at a time and rerunning them. Removing only the ownership check after the prompt's provider waits lets the demoted administrator's prompt complete a turn on bob's session (`"turn finished"` from his provider), once parked on the provider-update lock and once on the pending binding. Judging every scope by the stamp again fails the other two: the queued prompt runs a turn on bob's session (it reaches his provider), and the stale stamp rebinds bob's live session. Removing only the post-lock owner check restores bob's reaped chat session; judging only the ACP restore preload by the stamp recovers bob's interrupted turn into his history before the refusal; removing only the owner check in the resume closure rebinds bob's live session; judging only rehydration by the stamp revives bob's reaped session; removing only the scope from kill's durable fallback tombstones bob's session (`killed: true`), and from delete's fallback deletes it. The delete, kill and rehydration mutations ran on an earlier revision of these tests that lacked only the liveness precondition assertions. At that time, `git merge-tree --write-tree` with #10412 and `master` completed without conflicts; that historical check does not establish their current integration state. Did not run a live daemon against a real principal roster.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A: no rendered interface or presentation changed. The existing RPC denial shape is asserted by the handler regressions.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** Current hosted CI: `d5df4214cad96bfc6bfbdea13a64767b116ac1df` in the linked jobs. Historical local evidence remains `b0879527d3` on #11222's `69532f214e`. The current tests exercise handler and JSON-RPC dispatcher behavior, outbound frames, and storage effects. No live deployment or rendered-interface run is claimed.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** a refused request returns `{"code":-32012,"message":"Session not found or not owned by this principal"}` (`FORBIDDEN`), the same uniform denial scoped principals already receive; every regression asserts the code and message.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** A demoted administrator's queued prompt, close, delete, kill, configure, messages or resume of another principal's session is refused at the covered waits, with the foreign session's state preserved. Positive controls explicitly cover deletion and live/reaped resume of the caller's own sessions.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** In the historical local runs above, the `zeroclaw-plugins` legs and root-crate plugin tests were not repeated after the final RPC-only revision; the two runtime plugin legs were repeated. The current integrated head is covered by the linked hosted jobs, not a claim of repeated local execution. Docs gates were not run because no docs changed.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A. The change only narrows access: after a wait, cross-principal access requires the administrator bypass under the policy in force at that moment. Fixtures use the existing fake roster principals (`user:alice`, `user:bob`, uids 4242 and 4343).

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Wire/config shapes remain compatible; requests that lose authority while waiting are refused. Rust APIs add guarded `SessionBackend` methods and a generation field to `ResumedRpcSession`. The changed `resume_existing_authorized` callback is crate-private, not a public closure API.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- Backend compatibility: the new guarded disclosure and deletion defaults return `Unsupported`; custom persistent backends must implement them to support those RPC operations. The guarded state default has no persistent effect and authorizes the locked live owner; a backend that persists state must override it and read the stored owner under its mutation lock. In-tree SQLite and JSONL behavior is covered by the added tests. No wire or config migration is required.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert this PR's eventual squash commit; this reopens the reported bypass, so prefer a forward fix.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** session requests from principals whose authority did not change being refused after a wait: `FORBIDDEN` "Session not found or not owned by this principal" on their own sessions, or WARN "RPC authorization denied" for `session/close`, `session/kill`, `session/delete`, `session/configure` or `session/messages`.

v0.9.0 prioritizes opt-in OIDC dashboard sign-in, principal isolation, schema V4 and a CLI-only build option.

The standard build keeps the working in-process dashboard. Sign-in stays off by default, preserving the existing pairing flow. Source of truth: #7432 (https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/issues/7432), current release allocation. Existing implementation trackers keep their detailed work. Feature acceptance, current-head review/CI, recorded placement decisions and the v0.8.7-tag hold on breaking work remain in force.
