prs.title: fix(rpc): restore principal-owned Chat sessions after restart
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`.
- **Readiness:** Draft for review, blocked on integration and provider acceptance. GitHub reports conflicts against `master`; only labeling/risk automation has run, with no required code checks reported at publication. The recovery scenario passed in both corrected Keycloak attempts, but each complete Keycloak run still passed 22/23 because a different WebSocket-opening operation timed out. Authentik remains 11/19. No combined 23/23 result or milestone closure is claimed.
- **What changed and why:**
  - A remote owner could authenticate after daemon restart but `session/new` refused their persisted Chat session because its TUI binding existed only in the old process. Recover the exact RPC Chat row only when its durable principal and agent match the authenticated caller and requested agent.
  - Keep the restored candidate unpublished until history preparation succeeds. Recheck admission, live incarnation, durable owner, current permissions, workspace and environment at the relevant effects. Administrator privileges cannot substitute for durable ownership, and recovery cannot take another live TUI binding.
  - Guard restore-time history trimming inside the SQLite transaction, and hold a database-level owner-read boundary through live publication. RPC and gateway can open separate SQLite connections, so a connection-local mutex alone cannot fence another writer.
  - Add seven regression tests covering recovery, refusals, live bindings, administrators, queued/publication changes, guarded trimming and competing SQLite writers. Existing capacity/generation controls also run in the focused validation.
- **Scope boundary:** [Incremental repair](https://github.com/Aarlington/zeroclaw/compare/7d5d8f566d14cf3b7e4dc90446711d7a6c6c7fb7...85af504800c9062b18bf6c34e1d4cb33562c025d) on the tested OIDC stack (four files). Chat recovery only; no ACP recovery, token-validation relaxation, provider compatibility change, schema/config migration or milestone closure. Acceptance harness changes remain on a separate fork branch.
- **Blast radius:** RPC Chat restoration and the SessionStore publication helper; additive guarded transcript replacement in SessionBackend/SQLite; SQLite owner-read effects used by restoration and messages disclosure. Owner-read effects now briefly reserve the SQLite writer boundary across their synchronous callback.
- **Linked issue(s):** Depends on #11423. Related #8289. Related #10412 for overlapping agent-ownership admission work; its migration/claim contract must be reconciled when the stack converges.

### What this does, simply

After a restart, the daemon has forgotten its live sessions but still has their transcripts and owners on disk. This repair lets an authenticated owner reopen their own Chat history without a privileged local warm-up. Another user, an administrator who does not own the row, or a caller trying to take an existing live connection is still refused. If ownership or permissions change while recovery waits, the pending request cannot publish the session or trim its history under stale authority.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `cli` enrollment and Chat JSON-RPC (`channel=rpc`) over mTLS WebSocket; synthetic identities and disposable providers. Terminal rendering is not exercised.
- **Setup / preconditions:** SQLite session persistence, a configured OIDC provider, two mapped principals allowed to use the same agent, and nonempty Chat transcripts created through RPC. Use the pinned [acceptance harness](https://github.com/Aarlington/zeroclaw/tree/1916a099b1c064a7ffb4fb938402807d3cab7828/tests/manual).
- **Steps to run:** Create and read each principal's own transcript; retain signed TUI continuity; stop and restart the actual daemon; initialize with the same principal; call `session/new` with the existing ID and agent; read its messages. Attempt foreign messages/append/new/delete from the other principal and re-read both owners afterward. The harness case is `populated-principal-storage-survives-daemon-restart`; the workflow records setup, process identity and cleanup.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Both owners recover their exact nonempty transcripts; cross-principal attempts fail and leave the owners' data unchanged.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The old live-map check refuses the owner before durable restore. The executable red control uses the pre-repair RPC files from the tested stack, rather than claiming a current-master binary run.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [Fork validation run](https://github.com/Aarlington/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38602531986) verifies production-source equivalence, formatting, harness self-tests, 20 exact Rust regressions, the old-RPC regression control, four deliberate guard removals, strict Clippy for runtime/infra, and the shipped CLI build before the real-provider jobs. These are focused fork checks, not the upstream required PR gate.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Current-master integration and the eventual landed revision are not validated by this pinned-stack run. This is not the full workspace/all-features suite, cross-platform acceptance or an independent reviewer approval. Full two-provider acceptance failed: the final Keycloak attempt passed 22/23, with `signed-reconnect-and-stale-continuity-refusal` timing out while opening a WebSocket; Authentik passed 11/19 required cases and failed 8/19. Its failed cases are `client-credentials-cli-through-mtls-rpc`, `browser-pkce-cli-through-mtls-rpc`, `device-cli-through-mtls-rpc`, `wrong-audience-denied`, `unmapped-service-denied`, `offline-lifetime-cap-denied`, `introspection-deadline-and-revoked-reconnect`, `oidc-config-removal-and-restore-keeps-remote-closed`. The connection timeouts remain unresolved; no guard or timeout was relaxed, and token-purpose validation was not weakened.
- **Separate stack follow-up:** The [sop_workshop classification report on #11410](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/pull/11410#issuecomment-6124198437) remains open. Source review supports the missing constrained-principal classification and shared SOP write path; this recovery patch does not reproduce or repair that tool-authority concern.
- **Commands run and tail output:**
  - `cargo fmt --all -- --check`: exit 0.
  - `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/manual -p test_oidc_acceptance.py -v`: `Ran 23 tests`, `OK`.
  - `python3 tests/manual/oidc_exact_regressions.py`: 20 distinct named Rust tests; each selected exactly once, exit 0, `1 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored`.
  - `python3 tests/manual/oidc_recovery_controls.py`: old RPC owner-positive assertion fails with `-32003`; removing the final durable-owner guard, current-authority guard, trim authorization, or database transaction each causes a named assertion failure. Each control requires exit 101, one executed test, zero ignored, and an actual test failure. The old control corrects two test-only fixture details while retaining old RPC production code. Exact source bytes are restored afterward.
  - `cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-runtime -p zeroclaw-infra --lib --tests -- -D warnings`: exit 0 on restored source.
  - `cargo build --locked -p zeroclaw --bin zeroclaw`: exit 0.
  - Real-provider harness: Keycloak 22/23 required cases passed; Authentik 11/19. Counts include setup and cleanup. Both jobs verify the same binary artifact and SHA256. Required inventories, case order and timeouts are unchanged. The restart assertion now requires the exact expected refusal at each transport/durable-owner state and no success result; the previous assertion wrongly required FORBIDDEN before the foreign session was live. That failed run is retained, and all eight observed refusal codes are recorded.
  - Retry disclosure: the first corrected Keycloak run passed recovery but failed `unmapped-service-denied` on WebSocket opening timeout. One unchanged Keycloak-only retry reran all 23 cases against the same binary artifact: recovery and that unmapped-service case passed, but `signed-reconnect-and-stale-continuity-refusal` timed out at connection opening. Build/regression and Authentik receipts are from attempt 1; the final Keycloak result is attempt 2. Both full Keycloak runs remain failed; their cases are not combined into a green result. The timeout root cause has not been established.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Source self re-review traced identity, admission/constructor waits, final publication, history trimming, backend factory wiring, lock order, owner/agent restamping and unchanged live TUI policy. A separate receipt verifier reconciles raw named-test logs, failure reasons, provider inventories, job conclusions, exact heads and binary artifact upload/download digests. This is not an independent human review.
- **Visual interface evidence:** Exact final-interface output from CLI enrollment and daemon JSON-RPC receipts in the real-provider harness. No layout or renderer changes; protocol transition evidence is recorded below.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** Production `85af504800c9062b18bf6c34e1d4cb33562c025d`, harness `1916a099b1c064a7ffb4fb938402807d3cab7828`. [Build and provider logs](https://github.com/Aarlington/zeroclaw/actions/runs/38602531986) and artifacts `oidc-current-regressions`, `oidc-keycloak-evidence`, `oidc-authentik-evidence`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** Old owner recovery: `SESSION_NOT_OWNED` / `-32003`. Repaired Keycloak case: `populated-principal-storage-survives-daemon-restart` passed with two nonempty owner transcripts, unchanged private memory and bidirectional foreign-access refusal. No visual rendering claim.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** Actual daemon restart now permits durable Chat owner recovery; ownership/authority changes at tested effects prevent unauthorized publication or history mutation. Competing SQLite writes are blocked until the guarded effect ends, then permitted afterward.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Local Windows Rust tests were not used; Linux hosted execution supplies the Rust and real-provider receipts. Full workspace and cross-platform checks remain upstream integration gates. Earlier missing-component, fixture compile and superseded/cancelled runs are retained and do not count as final validation; an early red control that failed before the owner-positive assertion was rejected and corrected.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? Yes — authenticated remote principals can recover their own persisted Chat sessions when no live binding exists. Exact durable ownership, requested agent, current authority and live absence are required; administrator status cannot bypass ownership.
- New external network calls? No in production. Disposable provider calls are validation-only on the separate fork harness.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No; test identities and transcripts are synthetic.
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No.
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Recovery admits a previously blocked path to private history. Refusal, allowed-control, controlled-race, mutation and real-provider tests cover its ownership boundaries; legacy NULL-owner and unsupported stores fail closed.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? No for clients depending on the exact denial code from `session/new` for a missing-live foreign/legacy record: the existing `FORBIDDEN` code may now be returned where the live-map check previously returned `SESSION_NOT_OWNED`. Both remain opaque refusals. Persisted formats and successful existing live-session behavior are unchanged.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No.
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: Treat both `FORBIDDEN` (`-32012`) and `SESSION_NOT_OWNED` (`-32003`) as refusals; do not infer record existence from either. No database migration or configuration change is required. Authenticated recovery requires an already owned SQLite Chat row; ownerless histories are not adopted. Custom backends must implement guarded conversation replacement to support over-cap remote recovery; the default refuses that write.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** Revert the landed merge/squash commit with `git revert <landed-commit>`. Do not delete or rewrite durable transcripts. This returns remote restart recovery to the prior refusal and removes the new guards with the repair.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** An owner cannot reopen a known Chat session after restart; restore returns ownership/busy/internal errors; logs report `Failed to authorize session restore` or `Failed to persist Chat restore trim`. Check the supported local recovery path and retained transcripts before retrying; do not weaken ownership to force recovery.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A — no PR is superseded.

prs.title: fix(security): split POSIX commands at substitution and subshell boundaries
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master` (all contributions)
- **What changed and why:**
  - The shell command scanner split segments only at `;`, newlines, `|`, `||`, and `&&`, and split words only at whitespace. The closing `)` of `$(...)`, `<(...)`, `>(...)`, or a subshell, and the closing backtick of `` `...` ``, stayed glued to the last inner word. `x=$(cmd 2>/dev/null)` therefore produced the redirect target `/dev/null)`. That is not the null device, so with the default forbidden `/dev` the shell tool refused it: `Path blocked by security policy: /dev/null)`. #11469's exact null-device matching is correct and unchanged; the bad token came from the tokenizer.
  - Under the POSIX dialect, `split_unquoted_segments` now treats command substitution, process substitution, backticks, and subshells as segment boundaries, tracked on a frame stack so nesting and substitution inside double quotes work. The inner command becomes its own segment, and the enclosing word keeps a `$()`-style placeholder.
  - Every character other than those delimiters still lands in exactly one segment (heredoc bodies aside), including for unbalanced input. An unterminated `$(` still flushes the command around it, and a stray `)` (for example a `case` pattern terminator) is a boundary. A misparse can over-split but cannot drop text from the scan.
  - `<<` inside `$((...))` is a shift, not a heredoc. Previously `echo $((8<<1))` opened a heredoc that hid the following lines from the scan, though bash runs them. A command substitution nested inside arithmetic is ordinary shell syntax again, so its heredocs are recognized.
  - A substitution closes only at the `)` bash treats as its closer. A `case` pattern terminator, a `)` inside `${...}`, or a `)` inside a `#` comment no longer ends `$(...)` early. Closing early would restore the enclosing quote state and hide the rest of the inner command inside one quoted argument. Comment text is not syntax until the newline, so an apostrophe in a comment no longer opens a quote that hides the next line (separators inside comments still split, conservatively). This addresses review feedback in 4935b7a82.
  - The strict allowlist keeps rejecting unquoted POSIX grouping parentheses, so `(git status)` is not newly accepted as `git status` as a side effect of the split. Escaped and quoted parentheses (`find . \( ... \)`, `grep -E '(a|b)'`) are still allowed.
- **Scope boundary:** Does not change null-device classification (`is_null_device`, `is_safe_device_redirect_target`), the safe-redirect regexes, forbidden-path defaults, allowlists, or sandbox grants. `cmd.exe` and PowerShell splitting are unchanged. Not addressed here: `$(...)` inside an unquoted-delimiter heredoc body (bash runs it; the scanner still skips heredoc bodies by design), and `cmd.exe` parenthesized blocks.
- **Blast radius:** Every consumer of `split_unquoted_segments` under the POSIX dialect: the workspace path scan (`forbidden_path_argument*`) used by the shell, skill shell, and cron paths; `command_risk_level`; `is_command_allowed`; and `is_command_explicitly_allowed`.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #11469. Related #11823, Related #11824 (follow-ups for the scope this PR leaves out), Related #11825 (`zeroclaw-tools` test flake seen while validating).

### What this does, simply

Before running a shell command, ZeroClaw splits it into the individual commands it contains and checks each file path it mentions. That splitter didn't understand `$(...)`, backticks, or `(...)`, which are how shells run one command inside another. So in `x=$(ls 2>/dev/null)` it read the redirect target as `/dev/null)`, including the closing paren, and refused it as a forbidden path, even though #11469 made `/dev/null` always allowed. This was easy to hit, because `$(something 2>/dev/null)` is a very common shell idiom.

This PR teaches the splitter where those inner commands start and end. The inner command is checked on its own, so `2>/dev/null` inside it works again. As a side effect, commands hidden inside `$(...)` are now actually checked: a forbidden path inside `"$(...)"` is blocked, and `x=$(rm -rf ./build)` is rated high risk instead of low. Commands that the strict allowlist rejected before are still rejected.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes
- **Interface(s) exercised:** the `shell` tool, through any surface (`cli`, `tui`, or `web`)
- **Setup / preconditions:** Unix host, default `forbidden_paths` (includes `/dev`), `allowed_commands = ["*"]`, `block_high_risk_commands = false`
- **Steps to run:** Ask the agent to run each of these with the shell tool: `x=$(echo a 2>/dev/null); echo "$x"`, then `(echo a 2>/dev/null)`, then ``echo "`echo a 2>/dev/null`"``
- **Expected on this branch (after):** Each command runs and prints `a`.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** Each is refused with `Path blocked by security policy: /dev/null)` (or ``/dev/null` `` for the backtick form).

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** CI Required Gate (format, lint, Linux workspace tests, MSRV, Windows/macOS compile checks). The change is in `zeroclaw-config` policy parsing, plus one runtime shell-tool test.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** None specific. The behavior change is gated to `ShellDialect::Posix`, and a new test pins `cmd.exe` splitting as unchanged.
- **Commands run and tail output:** On `4935b7a82` (base `cdefa0d0a`), with the CI toolchain `1.98.0`:

```sh
$ cargo fmt --all -- --check
FMT_OK

$ cargo +1.98.0 clippy -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime --all-targets -- -D warnings
    Finished `dev` profile [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 1m 22s

$ cargo +1.98.0 test -p zeroclaw-config -p zeroclaw-runtime --lib
test result: ok. 1799 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
test result: ok. 5777 passed; 0 failed; 8 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out

# New end-to-end test against master's policy.rs (fix removed):
test tools::shell::tests::shell_allows_null_redirects_inside_posix_substitutions ... FAILED
x=$(echo zc-subst 2>/dev/null); echo "$x" must run, got: ToolResult { success: false, ..., error: Some("Path blocked by security policy: /dev/null)") }

# New policy tests against the unmodified tokenizer:
posix_segments_split_at_substitution_boundaries ... FAILED   left: ["x=$(echo a)"]
command_risk_level_sees_commands_inside_posix_substitutions ... FAILED   left: Low  right: High
forbidden_path_argument_allows_safe_devices_inside_posix_substitutions ... FAILED   left: Some("/dev/null)")
forbidden_path_argument_scans_inside_posix_substitutions ... FAILED   left: Some("/dev/nullx)")  right: Some("/dev/nullx")
```

- **Tests added or changed:**
  - `posix_segments_split_at_substitution_boundaries`: segment output for `$(...)`, `"$(...)"`, backticks, subshells, `<(...)`/`>(...)`, nesting, `$((...))`, unterminated and unbalanced input, quoted and escaped literals, and quotes inside a substitution.
  - `forbidden_path_argument_allows_safe_devices_inside_posix_substitutions`: 18 forms with `/dev/null` redirects inside substitutions, subshells, backticks, and process substitution, all allowed.
  - `forbidden_path_argument_scans_inside_posix_substitutions`: lookalikes (`/dev/nullx`, `/dev/null/../../etc/passwd`) and forbidden paths inside substitutions stay blocked and are reported without the closing `)`. This includes the double-quoted form, `case` bodies (quoted, unquoted, `(x)` patterns, after `then`, with a subshell in the body), `)` inside `${...}` and inside comments, a nested substitution in `${x:-...}`, a stray `)`, and the arithmetic-heredoc case.
  - `command_risk_level_sees_commands_inside_posix_substitutions`: `rm -rf` inside `$(...)`, `"$(...)"`, backticks, subshells, and `<(...)` is High; `x=$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null)` stays Low.
  - `strict_allowlist_still_rejects_posix_grouping_and_substitution`: the default strict policy still rejects `(git status)` and similar, and still allows escaped and quoted parentheses. Passes on both `master` and this branch.
  - `windows_cmd_does_not_split_posix_substitution_syntax`: `cmd.exe` splitting is unchanged.
  - `tools::shell::tests::shell_allows_null_redirects_inside_posix_substitutions`: the reported scenario end to end through `RateLimitedTool<ShellTool>` with the default forbidden `/dev`. A forbidden path inside `$(...)` is still refused and named without the `)`.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** Reproduced the original refusal in a live session on a binary that includes #11469. Checked the test fixtures against real `bash` (and `sh`, which is bash on the test host): a quote inside `"$(...)"`; a backtick inside double quotes running a command; `\$\(a\)` being literal while `\$(a\)` is a syntax error; `case` bodies running; and the line after `$((8<<1))` running, not being swallowed as a heredoc. Not verified: Windows execution (`cmd.exe` behavior is unchanged by construction and pinned by a unit test), and dash as `/bin/sh` (no POSIX-only constructs that dash treats differently are interpreted beyond what the tests cover).
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A. No user-visible interface state changed beyond the tool result shown above.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `4935b7a82`, `shell` tool via unit test `tools::shell::tests::shell_allows_null_redirects_inside_posix_substitutions`.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** See the command output above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** `x=$(echo zc-subst 2>/dev/null); echo "$x"` returns success with output `zc-subst`. On `master` it is refused with `Path blocked by security policy: /dev/null)`.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:**
  - Workspace-wide `cargo test` was not run. The diff is confined to `zeroclaw-config` and one `zeroclaw-runtime` test, and the only other crate calling these policy APIs is `zeroclaw-tools`.
  - `cargo test -p zeroclaw-tools --lib` passed (2092 passed with `--test-threads=1`) on the pre-rebase base `329e66f76`, not re-run after the rebase. In parallel it fails intermittently, in a different test on each run (`coding_agent_budget_tests::coding_agent_wrappers_charge_one_action_each`, `browser::tests::computer_use_dispatch_fails_closed_on_malformed_screenshot_response`), because a `codex_cli.rs` test sets the process-wide `PATH` to an empty directory. That is unrelated to this change.
  - Clippy on a newer local toolchain (`1.99.0`) reports `needless_borrows_for_generic_args` and `fetch_update` deprecations in untouched files (`zeroclaw-providers/src/lib.rs`, `zeroclaw-runtime/src/rpc/upload.rs`, `rpc/dispatch.rs`, `agent/turn/stream_guard.rs`). These are left to a separate PR; the CI toolchain `1.98.0` is clean.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? (`Yes`)
- New external network calls? (`No`)
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? (`No`)
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? (`No`)
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? (`No`)
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation:

prs.title: fix(config): stop migrating current-format configs that omit schema_version
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - **A config without `schema_version` was always read as version 1.** `detect_version` returned 1 for a missing key, so a hand-written or template-generated version 3 file that omits the key went through the version 1→version 3 migration in memory. Alias-keyed channel sections such as `[channels.discord.work]` and `[channels.discord.home]` collapsed into a synthesized `default` alias, and the rest were dropped. Nothing on disk changed and nothing was reported. A contributor lost their channel setup this way on a new laptop.
  - **The fix is to infer the current version when the shape is unambiguous.** A missing key is now read as version 3 when the file has no version 1-only top-level key, has at least one alias-keyed `providers.models.<family>` or `channels.<type>` section (every value a table), and has no such section holding fields directly, which is the version 2 shape. Anything else keeps the version 1 reading, so real version 1 and version 2 files migrate exactly as before.
  - **The inference is visible.** The loader records it on `Config::schema_version_inferred` and logs a WARN. The CLI prints a warning on stderr, next to the existing degraded-section warnings, telling the operator to add `schema_version = 3`.
  - **Our own templates now declare the version.** The release and Debian Dockerfiles wrote a default config with version 1 top-level keys (`api_key`, `default_provider`, `default_model`, `default_temperature`) and no `schema_version`, so every container start migrated it. The demo example was version 1-shaped too. Both are rewritten in version 3 shape with `schema_version = 3`, and each loads to the same `Config` as master's migration of the file it replaces. Adding only the key would have broken them: under version 3 the version 1 keys are unknown, and the provider would have been dropped.
  - **Nix and docs.** The Nix module's examples are now version 3 with `schema_version`, and its `settings` description says the module renders the attrset as written. The provider docs and the README tell people writing the file by hand to start it with `schema_version = 3`.
- **Scope boundary:** Quickstart is unchanged: it already writes `schema_version = 3`; see "How I tested". The Nix module does not inject `schema_version` into rendered settings, because a user's version 1-shaped `settings`, which its old documented example taught, would stop migrating. Version 1→version 3 and version 2→version 3 migration logic is unchanged. Channel-docs fragments are not touched, since they are snippets rather than whole files.
- **Blast radius:**
  - Config loading for files with no `schema_version`: `detect_version`, which is shared by the loader, `config migrate`, `ensure_disk_at_current_version`, and the pre-load filesystem-migration gate.
  - CLI stderr at startup.
  - The default config baked into the release and Debian images.
  - The demo harness config, the Nix module docs, and the provider docs.
- **Linked issue(s):** None filed. Reported by contributor tidux while setting up a new laptop.
- **Labels:** snapshot after labels are applied.

### What this does, simply

ZeroClaw's config file has changed shape twice. A `schema_version` line tells it which shape a file is in, and older files get converted automatically. Files from before the line existed have no version, so a missing line meant "oldest shape, convert it". But people who write a current-format file by hand, or copy one of our templates, often leave the line out. ZeroClaw then "converted" a file that was already current and lost settings, in particular every named channel alias except one, without any error.

After this PR, a file without the line that is clearly in the current format is read as current, and ZeroClaw prints a warning asking you to add the line. Files in the old formats are converted exactly as before. Our Docker images and demo config now include the line and use the current format.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** `Yes`
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `surface=cli`
- **Setup / preconditions:** an empty config dir.
- **Steps to run:** Write this as `<dir>/config.toml`, with no `schema_version`:
  ```toml
  [providers.models.ollama.default]
  model = "llama3"

  [channels.discord.work]
  enabled = true
  mention_only = true

  [channels.discord.home]
  enabled = true
  ```
  Then run `zeroclaw --config-dir <dir> config get channels.discord.work.mention_only`.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** prints `true`, and stderr carries the `no schema_version` warning naming the file.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** `Error: Unknown property 'channels.discord.work.mention_only'`. The same for `home`, and `channels.discord.default.enabled` prints `false`. The aliases were collapsed away in memory.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `CI Required Gate` passed on this head, `46ebd5df55` (run 36507405345), after a rebase onto master `1d64833a99`. It builds the root binary with the new CLI warning, runs the i18n catalogue and Fluent tests for the new `cli-config-schema-version-inferred` key, and runs the `zeroclaw-config` suite. The binary and the runtime i18n tests were not built locally, because the build host's disk is shared across many sessions.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** the Dockerfiles are exercised by the Docker jobs only when they run. Their config content is instead proven equal to the migrated original (below).
- **Commands run and tail output** (toolchain 1.98.0, this head):

```text
cargo +1.98.0 fmt --all -- --check                                               ok
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                           ok
cargo +1.98.0 test --locked -p zeroclaw-config --lib
    test result: ok. 1754 passed; 0 failed
cargo +1.98.0 clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-config --all-targets -- -D warnings    ok
BASE_SHA=$(git merge-base upstream/master HEAD) bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
    No blocking markdown issues on changed lines.
BASE_SHA=$(git merge-base upstream/master HEAD) bash scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
    No added HTTP(S) links detected in changed docs lines.
RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo +1.98.0 doc --locked --no-deps -p zeroclaw-config          ok
```

  New tests in `migration.rs`:
  - `a_plainly_current_file_without_the_key_is_read_as_current`
  - `an_inferred_current_file_keeps_every_channel_alias` (the contributor's case: `work` and `home` survive and no `default` is synthesized)
  - `an_explicit_version_is_never_reported_as_inferred`
  - `a_v2_shaped_file_without_the_key_keeps_the_v1_reading` (flat provider, flat channel, and mixed)
  - `a_v1_only_key_keeps_the_v1_reading`
  - `keys_shared_with_the_current_schema_do_not_veto_the_inference` (`cron`)
  - `a_file_with_no_alias_keyed_section_keeps_the_v1_reading`
  - `the_bundled_v1_fixture_is_still_read_as_v1`
  - `v1_keys_still_current_are_exactly_the_current_top_level_sections`, which guards the `V1_KEYS_STILL_CURRENT` exclusion list (`model_routes`, `embedding_routes`, `cron`) against schema drift.
- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?**
  - **What quickstart writes today.** With the released 0.8.5 binary, whose save and stamp code is identical to master's, both `zeroclaw quickstart --config-dir <fresh>` and `zeroclaw config set` into a fresh dir write `schema_version = 3` as the first line. On master, `Config::save` stamps it and keeps it through default-pruning (`SAVE_PRESERVE_KEYS`), and `save_dirty` stamps it on every incremental write. So configs without the key come from hand-written files and our templates, not from quickstart.
  - **The loss, reproduced.** With the 0.8.5 binary, the hand-written file above gives `Unknown property 'channels.discord.work.mention_only'`, while `channels.discord.default.enabled` gives `false`.
  - **Template equivalence.** A temporary, uncommitted test in `zeroclaw-config` loaded each new version 3 file (release Dockerfile, Debian Dockerfile, demo example) and master's `migrate_to_current` of the file it replaces. The two produced identical `Config` values: `docker.toml == docker.v3.toml: identical Config`, and the same for the Debian and demo files. The Nix example is master's migration of the old example, written as a Nix attrset. The demo keeps the `openrouter.agent_demo` and `channels.telegram.default` alias names that `demo/run-agent-host.sh` injects secrets into.
  - **Not verified locally:** the CLI warning's terminal output, since the root binary was not built here (CI builds it); the Docker images; and Nix evaluation.
- **Visual interface evidence:** `Exact plain-text output`: the warning is a single stderr line whose `en` text is in `crates/zeroclaw-runtime/locales/en/cli.ftl` (`cli-config-schema-version-inferred`).
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** local root-binary build and runtime i18n tests, which CI runs, because the host disk is shared.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? `No`
- New external network calls? `No`
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? `No`
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? `No`
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? `No`

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? `Yes`. Version 1 and version 2 files, with or without the key, migrate exactly as before. Only files that are plainly version 3 and lack the key change behavior: they now load as written instead of being migrated.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? `Yes`. There is a new stderr warning when the version is inferred, and the default config baked into the release and Debian images is now version 3-shaped, with the same effective `Config` as before.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? `No`
- Upgrade steps: none required. Operators who see the new warning should add `schema_version = 3` as the first line of their config.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert` the squash commit.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None. Adding `schema_version` to a config file removes any dependence on the inference.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** a version 1 or version 2 file wrongly read as version 3 would show `Unknown property` for its old top-level keys or unmigrated flat sections, together with the new `no schema_version` warning on stderr and in the WARN log.

prs.title: fix(config): trust platform roots for outbound WebSocket TLS
prs.body:
The current TLS behavior of Slack (and possibly other channel) is inconsistent. WebSocket connections trusted only the bundled Mozilla root certificates, but the HTTP clients also trust the OS certificate store.

Because of this, Slack Socket Mode failed behind a corporate proxy that inspects TLS. The REST calls passed. The WebSocket handshake failed.

This PR makes this consistent again. Both Slack HTTP and WSS trust the OS certificate store.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** Yes, if you have a proxy that inspects TLS.
- **Interface(s) exercised:** `channel` = `slack`
- **Setup / preconditions:** Configure the Slack channel. Route traffic through a proxy that re-signs TLS. Install the proxy CA in the operating system store, or set `SSL_CERT_FILE` to the CA file.
- **Steps to run:** Start the daemon. Watch the Slack channel connect.
- **Expected on this branch (after):** The connection to `wss-primary.slack.com` succeeds. Socket Mode events arrive.
- **Prior behavior on `master` (before):** The REST calls succeed. The WebSocket connection fails with `TLS handshake with wss-primary.slack.com`. The channel reconnects in a loop.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** Rust fmt, clippy, and test cover the changed crate. Docs Style covers the changed Markdown.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** rustfmt and clippy are not installed on my machine. CI must run them.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```sh
$ cargo test -p zeroclaw-config --lib
test result: ok. 1501 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 4.36s

$ DOCS_FILES=docs/book/src/channels/overview.md scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
Summary: 0 error(s)

$ DOCS_FILES=docs/book/src/channels/overview.md scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
No added links detected in changed docs lines.
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** A new unit test sets `SSL_CERT_FILE` to a test certificate. It checks that the root store has the Mozilla roots plus that one certificate. I did not test against a live Slack workspace behind a real proxy.
- **Visual interface changed?** N/A

prs.title: fix(transport): honor SSL_CERT_FILE for WebSocket connections
prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - Built-in WebSocket connections currently construct a trust store from bundled WebPKI roots only, so a private CA supplied through `SSL_CERT_FILE` is ignored and TLS-inspecting gateways can fail with an unknown issuer.
  - Load the explicitly configured PEM bundle for both direct and proxied secure WebSocket connections, adding its certificates to the existing bundled roots.
  - Reject unreadable, empty, malformed, or invalid bundles; retain certificate-chain, expiry, and hostname verification. Read the file on each new connection rather than caching its contents.
  - Add loopback TLS/WebSocket regression tests and document the environment-variable behavior. `rcgen` is test-only and already exists in the workspace lockfile.
- **Scope boundary:** No native OS-store discovery, `SSL_CERT_DIR`, client certificates, insecure verifier, provider HTTP changes, plugin transport changes, or proxy-routing changes.
- **Blast radius:** Built-in channel consumers of `ws_connect_with_proxy` when connecting to `wss://` with a non-empty `SSL_CERT_FILE`. Plain WebSocket behavior is unchanged.
- **Linked issue(s):** Related #9653 (the analogous trust-store gap on plugin HTTP; this PR addresses the separate built-in WebSocket path).

### What this does, simply

An operator can install a private CA for a local gateway or corporate TLS proxy, yet a channel's WebSocket connection still rejects that gateway because it only checks the certificates bundled into the binary. This change lets the operator point `SSL_CERT_FILE` at a trusted PEM bundle. WebSocket connections then recognize that CA while continuing to reject expired certificates and certificates for the wrong host. With the variable unset or empty, the existing bundled trust store is used as before.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A: the committed tests reproduce the changed transport boundary with local TLS and HTTP CONNECT endpoints, without channel credentials or an external service. Run the focused test command below.

### How I tested

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** [CI at e9fc8ae](https://github.com/zeroclaw-labs/zeroclaw/actions/runs/37038209028) passed the direct and HTTP CONNECT WebSocket CA integration tests, the no-default-features check, and the required aggregate gate. The separate Semgrep alert flags explanatory `ws://` documentation, not a new insecure connection path. Local validation below was performed on Linux ARM64 with Rust 1.96.0.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** Windows/macOS and SOCKS transport were not exercised locally. The proxied TLS branch was exercised through HTTP CONNECT. Full workspace tests were not run.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```sh
cargo fmt --all -- --check
# exit 0

cargo test --locked --release -p zeroclaw-config --features ws-transport --test websocket_ca
# test websocket_tls_client ... ok
# test direct_websocket_ca_policy ... ok
# test proxied_websocket_ca_policy ... ok
# test result: ok. 3 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored

cargo clippy --no-deps --locked --release -p zeroclaw-config --features ws-transport --all-targets -- -D warnings
# Finished release profile; exit 0

cargo check --locked --release -p zeroclaw-config --no-default-features
# Finished release profile; exit 0

DOCS_FILES=docs/book/src/reference/env-vars.md bash scripts/ci/docs_quality_gate.sh
# Summary: 0 error(s)

DOCS_FILES=docs/book/src/reference/env-vars.md bash scripts/ci/docs_links_gate.sh
# Ran 6 tests ... OK
# Checked 1 local docs link target(s).
# No added HTTP(S) links detected in changed docs lines.
```

The two transport tests each cover ten scenarios: trusted private certificate, unset/empty environment variable, wrong hostname, expired certificate, missing file, empty bundle, malformed PEM, invalid DER, and plain WebSocket with an unusable CA path. Clients run in separate processes so tests do not mutate the shared process environment. Certificates and keys are generated per test; no real certificates or credentials are committed.

The broader Clippy invocation **without** `--no-deps` was also attempted. It fails on the pre-existing `clippy::nonminimal_bool` at `crates/zeroclaw-infra/src/acp_session_store.rs:1648`. That file is byte-identical to the base `master` file (Git blob `89cbd0264878e56c5c16a1dd230021a301c006af`). The failure is an existing negated `is_some_and` expression that Clippy suggests writing as `is_none_or`; it is outside this transport fix. The scoped strict Clippy command above passes without suppressing lints in the changed crate.

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The original equivalent fix on v0.8.5 restored a Discord gateway connection through a private-CA TLS gateway, reaching READY. That smoke result is supporting evidence for the original deployment, not a claim of a live Discord test on this PR head.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A; no presentation changes.
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `e9fc8ae`; production `ws_connect_with_proxy` exercised by `crates/zeroclaw-config/tests/websocket_ca.rs`. The tested changed files were SHA-256 matched to the commit candidate. The final base refresh changed only `deny.toml` and an audit-policy document. Builds used two jobs and release overrides `opt-level=1`, `lto=false`, `codegen-units=16`, `debug=0`, `incremental=false`; docs gates ran in full-file mode.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** Test output above.
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** The private certificate reaches WebSocket HTTP 101 with the bundle configured, and is rejected without it. Wrong-host and expired certificates remain rejected on both connection paths.
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** Full workspace tests and cross-platform builds were omitted because this bounded change is covered at its real TLS/WebSocket boundary plus crate-level lint and feature checks. English documentation only; generated translation catalogs are unchanged.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? **Yes.** The WebSocket transport reads an operator-selected CA file and adds its trust anchors. Only use an operator-controlled bundle; this deliberately extends trust when the environment variable is explicitly set.
- New external network calls? **No.** Existing connection destinations and proxy selection are unchanged; regression tests use loopback only.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? **No.** The bundle contains public certificates; no client keys or channel credentials are read by the new code.
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? **No.**
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? **No.**
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: Additional CAs can authenticate peers. Bundled roots remain available, normal certificate and hostname verification stays enabled, unusable configured bundles fail closed, and file contents are resolved on each connection rather than cached.

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? **Yes for unset/empty `SSL_CERT_FILE`; explicitly configured values now affect WebSocket trust and invalid values fail connections.**
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? **Yes:** documented `SSL_CERT_FILE` support for built-in WebSocket TLS.
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? **No.**
- Exact upgrade steps: No action for the default behavior. For a private CA, set `SSL_CERT_FILE` in the daemon's environment to a readable PEM bundle and restart the process. Later bundle rotations take effect on new connections; existing connections are unchanged. Correct or unset an invalid pre-existing value.

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** After merge, revert the squash commit for #11443, rebuild, and redeploy.
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** Unset `SSL_CERT_FILE` and restart to restore bundled-only WebSocket trust. There is no new feature flag.
- **Observable failure symptoms:** WebSocket CA-bundle errors or TLS handshake/unknown-issuer errors; channel reconnection fails before WebSocket upgrade.

## Supersede Attribution (required only when `Supersedes #` is used)

N/A; this PR does not supersede another contribution.

prs.body:
## Summary

- **Base branch:** `master`
- **What changed and why:**
  - The plugin host's three egress dialers tried the resolved, policy-checked addresses one at a time, in resolver order, and moved on only when an address refused or was unreachable: `wasi:http` (`dial_pinned`), WebSocket (`dial_authorized`), and raw sockets (`connect_pinned`). An address that never answers, typically an IPv6 path that drops SYNs, therefore held the dial until the connect deadline ran out, and the next address (usually IPv4) was never tried. For a `wasi:http` request with no `connect_timeout`, that deadline was 600 s; the plugin call deadline (30 s by default) fired first, so every call failed as a call timeout. A Telegram channel plugin on a host whose IPv6 route to `api.telegram.org` loses SYNs stalled this way on every call, while `curl`, which races the two families, answered in half a second.
  - New shared helper `connect_pinned_addresses` (`crates/zeroclaw-plugins/src/egress.rs`). It dials the same pinned addresses, staggered in the style of RFC 8305 (Happy Eyeballs v2): address families alternate, starting with the first address's family; the next attempt starts when the previous one fails or after 250 ms without an answer; the first connection wins, and the attempts still pending are dropped, which closes their sockets before the dial returns. Every attempt shares one deadline, so several addresses still never multiply the caller's budget. All three dialers use it.
  - The race is bounded. It tries at most the first 8 addresses, after the families are interleaved, and keeps at most 4 attempts in flight at once. The resolver's answer has no size limit, and on a wildcard grant the plugin author may control the DNS, so a long answer can no longer multiply the half-open sockets one connection permit costs. The attempts are polled in place, not spawned as tasks, so returning or cancelling the dial drops them at once.
  - The TCP connect now has its own default, `DEFAULT_CONNECT_TIMEOUT` = 10 s. A `wasi:http` request without `connect_timeout` gets it in place of 600 s, and WebSocket and socket dials use it for their TCP stage. A `connect_timeout` the guest sets is still used exactly as given, shorter or longer. The response-stage defaults (first byte, between bytes) stay at 600 s, and the overall 30 s WebSocket and socket connect deadline still bounds TLS and the handshakes.
  - The WebSocket dialer keeps its existing fallback: if an address connects but TLS or the WebSocket handshake fails there, it moves on to the other addresses, racing them the same way. The 10 s connect budget is wall clock and covers all of these rounds, so time spent on a failed TLS or handshake comes out of it. If no later address connects, the TLS or handshake error is still the one reported. An address that refused in an earlier round is dialed again in the next one; a refusal costs one round trip.
- **Scope boundary:** The security contract is unchanged. Only the addresses the egress boundary resolved and validated are dialed, by `SocketAddr`; nothing is resolved again, and nothing outside the pin is reached. No error variant, WIT type, config key or dependency is added. The response-body path (`BetweenBytesTimeout`) is untouched.
- **Blast radius:** Every plugin egress connect: `wasi:http`, WebSocket, and TCP/TLS/STARTTLS sockets. A destination whose first address answers within 250 ms is dialed as before. On a path whose round trip is longer than 250 ms, a destination with several addresses now also gets a second connect attempt before the first answers, and the connection that loses is closed. A `wasi:http` request without `connect_timeout` whose destination never answers now fails as `connection-timeout` after 10 s instead of holding the call to its deadline. A slow but working TCP connect that takes more than 10 s now fails unless the guest raises `connect_timeout` (WebSocket and socket dials cannot raise it).
- **Linked issue(s):** Closes #11813
- **Release note:** Plugin network connections now stop waiting for a TCP connect after 10 s by default, instead of 600 s for `wasi:http` requests and 30 s for WebSocket and socket connections. A `wasi:http` plugin can still set its own `connect_timeout`; WebSocket and socket connections have no setting for it.

### What this does, simply

When a plugin connects to a server, the host first looks up the server's addresses, usually an IPv6 one and an IPv4 one, checks them against the operator's rules, and then connects. It used to try them strictly one after another, and if the first one never answered, the plugin waited for the whole timeout and never tried the second. On a network with a broken IPv6 route, a plugin could hang on every request even though IPv4 worked fine. The host now does what browsers and `curl` do: if the first address hasn't answered within a quarter of a second, it also tries the next one, and uses whichever connects first. It still only connects to the addresses it already checked, and it still gives up at the same overall deadline. It also stops waiting on an unanswered connect after 10 seconds by default, instead of 10 minutes.

## Testing (required)

### How you can test (when useful)

- **Reviewer testing requested?** N/A. The tests below reproduce a silent first address deterministically on loopback, and the race itself is tested with paused time.

### How I tested

- `egress::staggered_dial_tests` (paused tokio time, scripted connect step):
  - A silent first address is passed over after exactly 250 ms.
  - A refusal starts the next attempt at once.
  - All refused gives `Refused`.
  - All silent gives `TimedOut` at exactly the shared deadline, with attempts started at 0, 250 and 500 ms.
  - An address whose turn would come after the deadline is never dialed.
  - Twelve silent addresses: exactly four attempts start, at 0, 250, 500 and 750 ms, and the dial times out at the deadline.
  - Twelve refusing addresses: exactly the first eight are dialed. With ten IPv6 addresses and two IPv4 ones, the eight dialed still include both IPv4 addresses.
  - Families alternate from the first address.
  - Two attempts connect at the same instant while a third is still waiting: once the dial returns, only the winner's socket is open (a drop counter on each attempt's socket).
  - An empty set or a spent budget dials nothing.
- One path test per dialer, each in two variants: `[::1]:P` blackholed ahead of a live `127.0.0.1:P`, and the same over IPv4 alone. The blackhole is a loopback listener whose accept queue is full and never drained, so the kernel drops further SYNs.
  - `wasi_http::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_spend_the_connect_budget` and `..._over_ipv4`. `dial_pinned` takes raw addresses, so the IPv4 variant puts the blackhole on a second `127.0.0.1` port and runs on any host. Both also check that a pin holding only the silent address fails as `ConnectionTimeout` when a short guest budget runs out.
  - `component_websocket::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial` and `..._over_ipv4`, and `sockets::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial` and `..._over_ipv4`. An authorization pins one port, so these IPv4 variants use `127.0.0.2:P`, which is local on Linux.
  - A variant that cannot build its addresses on the host skips with the reason: no IPv6 socket, the bind failed, a connect failed while the queue filled, or the queue never filled.
- `component_websocket::tests::only_silent_addresses_time_out_at_the_connect_default`: with only a blackholed address, the dial ends as `Timeout` after the 10 s default (paused time).
- `component_websocket::tests::a_tls_failure_is_reported_over_a_later_connect_failure`: an address that connects but fails TLS, followed by one that refuses, reports `TlsFailed`.
- `sockets::tests::a_dial_that_reaches_no_address_is_a_failed_connect`: refused and silent addresses both give `ConnectFailed`, the silent one after the 10 s default.
- `wasi_http::tests::unset_timeouts_take_the_connect_default_and_the_earlier_stage_timeouts`: the 10 s connect default, with a guest's own 2 s and 60 s kept as given.

With this change's tests and helper, but the three dialers and the connect default as on `master`:

```text
test wasi_http::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_spend_the_connect_budget ... FAILED
test wasi_http::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_spend_the_connect_budget_over_ipv4 ... FAILED
  the reachable address must connect within the budget: ErrorCode::ConnectionTimeout
test component_websocket::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial ... FAILED
test component_websocket::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial_over_ipv4 ... FAILED
  left: Err(Elapsed(()))   right: Ok(Ok(()))
test sockets::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial ... FAILED
test sockets::tests::a_blackholed_first_address_does_not_hold_up_the_dial_over_ipv4 ... FAILED
  the silent address must not stall the dial: Elapsed(())
test component_websocket::tests::only_silent_addresses_time_out_at_the_connect_default ... FAILED
  left: Err(Elapsed(()))   right: Ok(Err(Timeout))
test sockets::tests::a_dial_that_reaches_no_address_is_a_failed_connect ... FAILED
  gave up after 30.001s
test wasi_http::tests::unset_timeouts_take_the_connect_default_and_the_earlier_stage_timeouts ... FAILED
  left: SendTimeouts { connect: 600s, .. }   right: SendTimeouts { connect: 10s, .. }
test result: FAILED. 15 passed; 9 failed
```

With the change, all 24 selected tests pass in about 1 s. Each guard was also checked on its own. Without the address cut, the two eight-address tests fail. Without the in-flight cap, the four-attempt test fails (eight start). With the attempts spawned as tasks instead of polled in place, the drop-counter test finds two sockets still open when the dial returns.

Against the real API: the released Telegram channel plugin 0.4.0, bound with a fake bot token, ran under a daemon built from `master` and then under one built with this change, for 240 s each. The host had the failure #11813 describes: during each run a side probe saw about one IPv6 connect in ten to `api.telegram.org` time out, while every IPv4 connect succeeded. The daemon's sockets to port 443 were sampled every 0.5 s:

| Build | Poll calls that hit the 30 s call deadline | Socket samples (state and family) |
|---|---|---|
| `master` | 4 | 256 `SYN-SENT` IPv6, 63 `ESTAB` IPv6, never IPv4 |
| this change | 0 | 64 `SYN-SENT` IPv6, 154 `ESTAB` IPv6, 6 `SYN-SENT` IPv4, 24 `ESTAB` IPv4 |

On `master` a lost IPv6 SYN held the call until its deadline, and IPv4 was never tried. With this change the same losses fall back to IPv4, and no call reached the deadline. The plugin logs nothing on the 401 its fake token earns, and channel health reads `error` with either build for that reason, so the comparison rests on the deadline failures and the dialed families. The token appears in no saved log.

- **CI checks relied on and why they cover this change:** `Check (plugins cranelift backend)` runs the plugins lib unit tests and the component tests (`egress_plugin_e2e`, `socket_plugin_e2e`, `websocket_plugin_e2e`, …), and the runtime leg runs the root `channel_egress_e2e` and `channel_websocket_e2e`. `Lint` covers clippy.
- **Known CI coverage gap, if any:** The IPv6 path tests need `::1`, and the WebSocket and socket IPv4 variants need `127.0.0.2` to be local (Linux). A runner missing either skips those variants with the reason; the `wasi:http` IPv4 variant and the scripted race tests run everywhere.
- **Commands run and tail output:**

```text
cargo fmt --all -- --check                                                                  exit 0
cargo clippy --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --all-targets -- -D warnings                      exit 0
  (also with --features plugins-wasm-cranelift; --no-default-features with plugins-wasm-cranelift,
   plugins-wasmtime and plugins-wasm-pulley)                                               exit 0 each
cargo clippy --locked --workspace --exclude zeroclaw-desktop --all-targets --features ci-all -- -D warnings   exit 0
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --no-default-features --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --lib
  test result: ok. 435 passed; 0 failed
cargo test --locked -p zeroclaw-plugins --features plugins-wasm-cranelift
  517 passed, 0 failed across 14 targets (egress_plugin_e2e, socket_plugin_e2e, websocket_plugin_e2e, ...)
cargo test --locked --features plugins-wasm-cranelift --test channel_egress_e2e --test channel_websocket_e2e --test plugin_channel_runtime_e2e
  19 passed, 0 failed
bash scripts/ci/comment_hygiene_gate.sh                                                     passed
```

- **Beyond CI, what did you manually verify?** The real-API comparison above. I did not run the WebSocket or socket paths against a real service; their tests are loopback only.
- **Visual interface evidence:** N/A
- **Tested revision, interface, and evidence path:** `master` at `4e82ce46e9` plus this diff, Linux x86_64.
- **Screenshot or exact-output evidence:** N/A
- **Action or changed state and observed result:** N/A
- **If any command was intentionally skipped, why:** none.

## Security & Privacy Impact (required)

- New permissions, capabilities, or file system access scope? No
- New external network calls? No. The same validated addresses are dialed; some are now dialed concurrently, and the attempts that lose are dropped.
- Secrets / tokens / credentials handling changed? No
- PII, real identities, or personal data in diff, tests, fixtures, or docs? No
- Prompt injection or untrusted model-visible text introduced/changed? No
- If any `Yes`, describe the risk and mitigation: N/A

## Compatibility (required)

- Backward compatible? Yes, with one bound change: a `wasi:http` request without `connect_timeout`, and every WebSocket and socket dial, now gives the TCP connect 10 s, where `wasi:http` previously allowed 600 s and the other two 30 s. A guest that needs longer can set `connect_timeout`.
- Config / env / CLI surface changed? No
- Rust/MSRV/toolchain floor changed? No
- If backward compatibility is `No` or either surface/floor question is `Yes`: exact upgrade steps for existing users: N/A

## Rollback (required for medium/high-risk PRs)

- **Fast rollback command/path:** `git revert <sha>`
- **Feature flags or config toggles:** None
- **Observable failure symptoms:** Plugin calls ending at `plugin call exceeded wall-clock deadline` while `curl` reaches the same host, or sockets stuck in `SYN-SENT` toward one address family (`ss -tnpo`).
